input.title: Right-Ankle Running Rehabilitation Historical Chronology — January–April 2027
input.body:
RIGHT-ANKLE RUNNING REHABILITATION: HISTORICAL CHRONOLOGY
January–April 2027

Prepared/documented: January 1, 2028
Patient: Riley Tanaka
Body region: Right ankle

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This document summarizes the recorded history of the January–April 2027 right-ankle return-to-running rehabilitation, including session structure, spacing, during-session and later-that-day symptom checks, and following-day ordinary walking and stair observations. It is a historical record for clinician review. It is not a current activity clearance, a statement of present ankle status, or a new progression recommendation. Any present running, cycling, or rehabilitation decisions should come from the treating clinician’s current assessment.

KEY HISTORICAL SYMPTOM LANGUAGE
The monitored concerns were focal right-ankle pain/ache, swelling, instability, and gait change. Sessions were to stop for focal pain or a gait change rather than pushing through. A session was treated as tolerated only after the later-that-day check and the following-day check, including ordinary walking and stairs, remained symptom-free.

CHRONOLOGY

December 26, 2026 — Pre-period event relevant to the January restart
During the third running interval of a prescribed 20-minute run-walk session, a focal ache on the inside of the right ankle began, approximately 2/10. The session was stopped; the ache settled in about 10 minutes. There was no swelling, instability, visible injury, or gait change. Running was then paused pending assessment.

January 8, 2027 — Rehabilitation follow-up and interim status
At the follow-up, the recent focal medial/right-ankle ache and the December 26 interruption were reviewed. Necessary walking had remained symptom-free, and there had been no running since December 26. The interim record limited activity to necessary symptom-free walking until updated clinical guidance. Ankle-and-calf strengthening was continued separately; the strengthening blocks did not themselves authorize running.

January 23–24, 2027 — Walking prerequisite/test
After 14 consecutive symptom-free days, a 30-minute brisk-walk test was completed on January 23, with an easy start and post-walk check. There was no pain or gait change during the walk, later that day, or through January 24. This was documented as a prerequisite/check, not as permission for unrestricted running.

January 26, 2027 — Initial run-walk restart, session 1
Structure: 20 minutes total, four rounds of 4-minute easy running alternating with 1-minute walking. Spacing: limited to two nonconsecutive running sessions per week; no third session. During-session and later-that-day checks: no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change. Following-day check through January 27: ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free.

January 30, 2027 — Initial run-walk restart, session 2
Structure: the same 20-minute pattern of 4-minute easy runs alternating with 1-minute walks. Spacing: nonconsecutive sessions, with no third weekly session. The contemporaneous plan retained the stop-for-focal-pain-or-gait-change rule and the later-that-day/following-day checks. The January 30 session and its subsequent check were recorded as symptom-free; ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through January 31.

February 2, 2027 — Initial run-walk restart, session 3
Structure: the same 20-minute 4-minute easy-run/1-minute-walk intervals. During-session and later-that-day checks: no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change. Following-day check through February 3: ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free. This was the third of six required symptom-free sessions at this level.

February 6, 10, and 13, 2027 — Completion of the 20-minute run-walk block, sessions 4–6
Each session used the same 20-minute structure: 4-minute easy runs alternating with 1-minute walks. Sessions remained nonconsecutive, with no third weekly session. Each session was checked during the intervals and later that day for focal pain, swelling, instability, and gait change, followed by a next-day check including ordinary walking and stairs. All three sessions and following-day checks were recorded as symptom-free. Together with January 26, January 30, and February 2, these completed six symptom-free 20-minute run-walk sessions.

February 19, 2027 — Interval-progression clinical review
The review documented six symptom-free 20-minute run-walk sessions and their following-day checks. The next historical rehabilitation level was two nonconsecutive 25-minute sessions per week, alternating 9-minute easy runs with 1-minute walks. Six symptom-free sessions at that level were required before continuous running; the former 40-minute baseline remained suspended.

February 21, 24, and 28; March 3, 7, and 10, 2027 — 25-minute run-walk block
Six nonconsecutive 25-minute sessions were completed using 9-minute easy runs alternating with 1-minute walks:
- February 21 — session and later-that-day check symptom-free; following-day check symptom-free.
- February 24 — same structure and symptom-free checks.
- February 28 — same structure and symptom-free checks.
- March 3 — same structure and symptom-free checks.
- March 7 — same structure and symptom-free checks.
- March 10 — same structure; symptom-free during the session and later that day; ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through March 11.

Across this block there was no reported focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change. Ankle-and-calf strengthening continued three times weekly, and no third weekly run was added. Continuous running remained deferred pending clinical review.

March 15, 2027 — Clinical check and transition to continuous running
After the six symptom-free, nonconsecutive 25-minute run-walk sessions, the clinical check documented clearance at that time for two nonconsecutive 30-minute continuous easy runs per week. The session-plus-following-day symptom check continued. The former 40-minute running baseline and a third weekly run were not included in that historical clearance.

March 17 and 21, 2027 — First post-review continuous-run sessions
Two nonconsecutive 30-minute continuous easy runs were completed. During each run and later that day there was no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through the following-day checks on March 18 and March 22. Ankle-and-calf strengthening continued; no third weekly session was added.

March 24, 2027 — Additional 30-minute continuous run
The continuous easy run stayed at 30 minutes. There was no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through March 25. No 40-minute run or third weekly session was added.

April 4, 7, 11, and 14, 2027 — April continuous-run block
Structure and spacing: four 30-minute continuous easy runs, kept at two nonconsecutive sessions per week. No 40-minute run and no third weekly session were attempted. Ankle-and-calf strengthening continued three times weekly.

- April 4: no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day; following-day ordinary walking and stairs symptom-free.
- April 7: same during-session, later-that-day, and following-day findings.
- April 11: same during-session, later-that-day, and following-day findings.
- April 14: same during-session and later-that-day findings; ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through the April 15 check.

The corrected running log identifies April 4, April 7, April 11, and April 14 as the four April sessions. An earlier preliminary account listed April 4, April 8, and April 12; the corrected April 15 record superseded that preliminary date list.

April 16, 2027 — Follow-up context
A follow-up was scheduled to review the running history and address outdoor bike commuting separately. The historical running record above should not be interpreted as clearance for outdoor cycling, 40-minute running, a third weekly run, or any current activity.

HISTORICAL RESPONSE SUMMARY
- January 26 through February 13: six symptom-free 20-minute run-walk sessions, nonconsecutive, using 4-minute easy runs/1-minute walks.
- February 21 through March 10: six symptom-free 25-minute sessions, nonconsecutive, using 9-minute easy runs/1-minute walks.
- March 17 through April 14: 30-minute continuous easy runs at two nonconsecutive sessions per week, with no reported focal pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during or later the same day, and symptom-free ordinary walking and stairs at the following-day checks documented through April 15.
- The record describes what occurred in 2027; it does not establish current tolerance or current clearance as of the January 1, 2028 document date.

CLINICIAN REVIEW NOTE
Please use this chronology as patient-reported historical rehabilitation data and reconcile it with the current examination, current symptoms, treatment plan, and any intervening events before making activity decisions.

input.title: Hypothesis-number crosswalk — Mid-segment churn investigation (Feb–Apr 2023)
input.body:
Purpose
Compact decoding reference for numbered hypothesis mentions in the archived “Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned.” Preserve this ordering; do not renumber or substitute later labels.

H1 — Pricing artifact
Packaging, discounting, or contract-mix effects. This is separate from Marcus’s pricing-page experiment. The tier cut was essentially flat (Entry 5.0%, Standard 5.2%, Plus 5.1%), so H1 was ruled out.

H2 — Competitor cycle
Whether a competitor targeted the mid-segment base; the related generic-seasonality explanation was considered alongside it. Same-window February comparisons found no matching spike (2021: 2.0%; 2022: 2.2%), so H2 was ruled out.

H3 — Onboarding timing
Whether late-December/early-January starts convert to churn on a lag, especially when the day-7 onboarding touch is scheduled by calendar day rather than activation state. The activation-day rerun found 3.1% churn for users activating before the touch versus 7.8% for the post-day-7 pre-activation bucket (n=210); the follow-on onboarding-trigger experiment was the intervention track.

H4 — CS coverage gap
Whether CSM load or coverage drift explains the spike.

Decoding rule
“H1” through “H4” refer only to the four hypotheses above, in this original order. In particular: H1 is not the pricing-page experiment; H2 is not a general claim about all seasonality; H3 is onboarding timing; H4 is CS coverage.

# Helio Start leadership readout — Jun 22

## Current call
Helio Start is a working name for the sub-50-seat motion. It is still pre-discovery, not a pricing-page launch, beta, or cheap-plan promise.

## Gate newly added from engineering scoping
Before any pricing-page experiment or launch, we need clean event taxonomy and entitlement instrumentation for admin complexity, import or migration help, support handoff, and entitlement state. Any later pricing-page test also needs to obey the no-concurrent-layout/UI-change rule.

## Baseline measurement spine
Use activation definition v3. Keep 75-200-seat mid-seg v2 separate. Show the 50-75-seat band separately. The descriptive baseline: simple under-50 deployments with a first-week first integration behave near the target range, while permissions/import/billing/migration complexity lags by more than 15 points.

## Decisions needed this week
1. Accept instrumentation as a hard gate before pricing-page experiment or launch.
2. Keep billing exceptions and manual import/migration needs in the refusal-risk model for June.
3. Keep lifecycle work at fork mapping until eligibility and state-changing paths are clearer.

## Not decisions this week
No public pricing-page copy. No Q3 launch commitment. No change to retained-mid expansion-nudge eligibility.

## Open questions
Engineering: event taxonomy, entitlement state, dashboarding, and sizing.
Lifecycle: where the onboarding path must fork without creating support promises.
Support: which handoffs are allowed for the first self-serve shape and which remain assisted.

After I presented the matured GA, six-cohort activation, and connector-check evidence, Marcus asked Helio to open a paid-acquisition test and attach a Q3 pipeline target. I argued that the evidence establishes safe organic operation and useful activation, not durable retention or forecastable revenue. Tomás and Priya decided that Helio Start will remain available as an ongoing organic pricing-page channel through Q3, with the existing refusal rules and connector-access check intact. They declined the paid test and pipeline target and require first-paid and day-90 retention evidence before reconsidering those uses. I’m sharing the settled decision; no response is needed.

input.title: Helio Start change-sequencing checklist — 2028-01-01
input.body:
Helio Start change-sequencing checklist
As of: 2028-01-01

Purpose
Keep packaging, pricing-page work, acquisition, lifecycle changes, and activation reporting interpretable. A downstream item stays blocked until the prerequisite immediately above it is settled and QA-verified.

Sequence at a glance
1. Eligibility and refusal boundaries
2. Packaging and entitlement policy
3. Measurement taxonomy and canonical entitlement instrumentation
4. Pricing-page experiment readiness
5. Lifecycle fork and support-routing readiness
6. Paid-acquisition case, if separately approved
7. Activation measurement and reporting

1. Eligibility and refusal boundaries
Prerequisite to settle first:
- Lock the canonical Helio Start eligibility band and seat-count definition.
- Define supported versus unsupported features and services.
- Decide refusal, Sales-assist, and human-handoff rules, including admin ownership, connector access, permissions, billing exceptions, and import/migration help.
- Define which support handoffs are allowed and which cases remain outside self-serve.

Downstream work blocked until settled:
- Packaging: do not turn an unresolved operating boundary into a customer-facing package or promise.
- Pricing-page experiment: do not expose or test an offer whose eligible population and assisted path are still ambiguous.
- Lifecycle fork: do not build state-changing branches or copy before eligibility and routing are known.
- Paid acquisition: do not buy traffic into an undefined or unsupported path.

2. Packaging and entitlement policy
Prerequisite to settle first:
- Convert the approved eligibility/refusal policy into a stable package definition: who qualifies, what is included, what is excluded, and when an account is entitled.
- Define the canonical entitlement state and effective-date behavior for later billing or support changes.
- Obtain Billing sign-off on the supported billing path; do not assume a new billing term or redesign billing as part of discovery.
- Produce customer-safe packaging language that does not imply GA, universal under-50 eligibility, unsupported imports, or a public self-serve path where those are not approved.

Downstream work blocked until settled:
- Pricing-page experiment: the test cannot run against changing package semantics or an unapproved entitlement path.
- Lifecycle fork: onboarding and education cannot safely branch on an unsettled package or state.
- Paid acquisition: ads, landing pages, and spend cannot promote an offer whose eligibility, billing, or fulfillment is not fixed.
- Activation measurement: cohort assignment and denominators cannot be trusted without a canonical admission/entitlement rule.

3. Measurement taxonomy and canonical entitlement instrumentation
Prerequisite to settle first:
- Define and validate the event taxonomy for the relevant funnel stages.
- Instrument canonical entitlement state, not manually maintained spreadsheet tags.
- Capture clean properties for admin complexity, import/migration help, support handoff, and entitlement state.
- Verify that self-serve-eligible accounts can be separated from Sales- or CS-assisted accounts.
- Complete backfill/QA evidence and confirm that the new-workspace path is clean.

Downstream work blocked until settled:
- Pricing-page experiment: no customer-facing test or launch before taxonomy and entitlement measurement are clean and validated.
- Activation measurement: no reliable cohort, activation denominator, or support-dependent cut before the source states are trustworthy.
- Paid acquisition: no defensible attribution or paid-cohort comparison while eligible, assisted, and refused paths cannot be separated.

4. Pricing-page experiment
Prerequisite to settle first:
- Complete Sections 1–3.
- Freeze the hypothesis, primary metric, eligible population, treatment assignment, duration, and stop/read rules.
- Get Billing sign-off and confirm the entitlement path is QA-clean.
- Do not change pricing-page layout/UI, signup layout, taxonomy, dashboard logic, or entitlement logic concurrently with the experiment; otherwise the read is confounded.
- Keep Helio Start exposure bounded to the explicitly approved path. Design exploration may continue separately, but it is not evidence of launch readiness.

Downstream work blocked until settled:
- Experiment readout or pricing/launch decision: no causal or commercial interpretation from a contaminated or mixed-population window.
- Paid acquisition: do not scale or buy traffic based on an uninterpretable pricing-page result.
- Packaging changes: do not revise package meaning during the test unless the experiment is stopped and reset as a new change window.

5. Lifecycle fork and support-routing readiness
Prerequisite to settle first:
- Complete Sections 1–3.
- Define the lifecycle fork from canonical eligibility, entitlement, activation state, and support/refusal routing.
- Decide which touches are informational/non-state-changing and which require manual review; no proxy automation for state-changing branches.
- Keep lifecycle QA, support capacity, and handoff behavior observable.
- Avoid running activation/retention, lifecycle-email, and feature-flag changes concurrently when that would create a noisy read.

Downstream work blocked until settled:
- Paid acquisition: lifecycle fork must exist before paid traffic; otherwise acquisition changes both demand and an unresolved onboarding/support treatment.
- Activation interpretation: do not attribute movement to product or acquisition while lifecycle treatment is changing without a frozen comparison.
- Broader exposure: do not expand beyond the bounded path while support routing and lifecycle behavior are unproven.

6. Paid acquisition
Prerequisite to settle first:
- Treat paid acquisition as a separate experiment, not an automatic consequence of organic or beta evidence.
- Obtain explicit approval for spend, audience, attribution, cohort cap, and stop rules.
- Require mature first-paid and day-90 retention evidence together with refund-adjusted cash and account-level support effort; first-paid, activation, or paid-active status alone is insufficient.
- Define the paid cohort and compare it on the same mature status, cash, and support measures as the relevant organic cohort.
- Confirm the lifecycle fork, eligibility/refusal rules, connector-access check, entitlement instrumentation, and support capacity are unchanged and ready.

Downstream work blocked until settled:
- Any paid campaign, paid-social/search test, pipeline target, or forecast credit.
- Any claim that organic Helio Start evidence proves paid acquisition cost, incremental attribution, paid-cohort quality, or paid support economics.

Current boundary:
- Helio Start remains a bounded organic pricing-page channel unless a separate paid case clears this gate. Do not treat this checklist as paid-traffic authorization.

7. Activation measurement and reporting
Prerequisite to settle first:
- Lock the activation definition (use activation definition v3 where applicable), admission rule, observation window, and denominator policy.
- Assign the Helio Start cohort from creation-time entitlement/admission; apply later support or billing changes at their effective timestamps.
- Keep unresolved support state as “pending support state,” preserve raw events/timestamps, and exclude unresolved rows from support-dependent cuts or report them explicitly as pending.
- Require complete day-7/day-14 windows before calling a cohort mature, as applicable to the read.
- Create separate saved views/dashboard tiles before the next candidate enters: one Helio Start activation view and one retained-mid view.

Downstream work blocked until settled:
- Any activation rate, support-load rate, or lifecycle read that mixes admitted self-serve accounts with refused/assisted cases or incomplete windows.
- Any comparison with ordinary starter, retained mid-segment, or Expansion Assist denominators.
- Any use of activation as a proxy for mature conversion, retention, revenue, forecastable pipeline, or paid-acquisition readiness.

Required population separation
- Helio Start activation is its own controlled-beta/operating readout.
- Do not merge Helio Start with retained mid-seg, ordinary starter, or Expansion Assist populations, metrics, dashboards, or denominators.
- Keep sub-50 Helio Start distinct from the 50–75-seat band and the 75–200-seat retained-mid segment.
- Keep admitted self-serve accounts distinct from refused, Sales-/CS-assisted, routed-before-setup, and unresolved/pending-support cases.
- Report exposure/admission separately from activation outcomes; do not let pricing-page exposure or lifecycle-touch counts redefine the activation denominator.
- Keep Helio Start activation and support-load reporting as learning/operating evidence, not a blended revenue motion.

Final release check
[ ] Eligibility/refusal and assisted-routing boundaries are signed off.
[ ] Packaging, billing path, and canonical entitlement semantics are fixed.
[ ] Event taxonomy and entitlement instrumentation are QA-clean.
[ ] Pricing-page test population, hypothesis, treatment, and change-free window are frozen.
[ ] Lifecycle fork and support routing are defined and QA-approved.
[ ] Paid acquisition, if proposed, has separate spend, attribution, stop rules, and mature-evidence approval.
[ ] Activation definition, windows, denominators, and pending-state treatment are documented.
[ ] Helio Start, retained-mid, ordinary starter, and Expansion Assist reporting remain separate.

Hold the affected row and fail closed. Do not release it, queue it, include it in a send manifest, or treat the existing preflight as approval evidence.

2. Source correction

Route the correction through the responsible source owner in the authoritative source. Preserve the original row, correction provenance, source snapshot/as-of time, owner, correction timestamp, and validation result.

A source refresh or reconciliation alone does not authorize release. After the correction is confirmed, the affected row must undergo a fresh, row-level eligibility, suppression, state, and message preflight against the current authoritative views.

3. Prohibited workaround

Do not resolve the discrepancy through a template-only change, report-level override, manual hold clearing, or favorable-value selection. A template change may not substitute for correcting or reconciling the authoritative source state.

4. Unaffected audience

The unaffected audience may proceed only as a separately evaluated audience, after its own complete current preflight passes under the existing authority model. That preflight must confirm current source values, freshness, eligibility, suppression, recipient mapping, template/rendering behavior, and any applicable Customer Success or incident checks.

The unaffected audience is not grandfathered by the prior result, and it may not inherit the affected row’s correction, exception, or release decision. Any missing, stale, conflicting, or ambiguous check keeps the relevant audience held.

5. Authority boundary

This ruling preserves existing ownership and does not expand or transfer authority:

- The source owner performs and certifies the source correction.
- Ines retains the ordinary lifecycle messaging preflight and bounded routine-release lane.
- Daniela’s engineering release and rollback controls remain unchanged.

input.title: Warehouse glossary — activation definition v2
input.body:
Activation definition v2

Status: Retired for new/current reporting; preserved for historical analysis and comparison.

Exact criteria
An account is activated under v2 when both conditions are met within 14 days of the cohort/start anchor:
- It completes its first integration.
- It logs in at least twice (the historical wording is “logged in twice”) within that same 14-day window.

Do not substitute activation definition v3 criteria for v2 rows or labels. v3 is a different definition: completed first integration plus at least one qualifying in-product event within 14 days.

Active-cut period
v2 was the active activation cut from November 2022 until its replacement by activation definition v3 during the March 2023 transition. The historical record identifies v2 as “Nov 2022 onward” before v3 shipped, and identifies v3 as shipping in March 2023; it does not establish a more precise v2 retirement timestamp. When the exact cutover timestamp is required, use the versioned warehouse metadata rather than inferring it from report dates.

After replacement
- Do not delete, overwrite, relabel, or recompute historical v2 values as v3.
- Keep v2 in separately named, versioned warehouse tables/views and retain its original labels and historical values.
- Keep v2 available as a clearly labeled comparison series for historical cohort comparisons and reconciliation.
- New/current activation reporting should use the replacement definition of record (v3), with the definition version, 14-day window, cohort basis, and data freshness shown explicitly.
- Any analysis combining v2 and v3 must identify the definition change and must not present the two rates as directly comparable without an explicit reconciliation.

Source notes
- Historical v2 criterion: first integration + two logins in 14 days.
- Historical v2 active start: November 2022.
- Replacement direction: v3 uses first integration + at least one qualifying in-product event within 14 days.
- Preservation rule: retain v2 as a separately named comparison series; do not overwrite v2 labels or historical values.

results.content:
Using the terms previously recorded:

- Annual-fee card: $150 annual fee
- Travel credit: $75, if fully usable
- No-fee card: $0 annual fee
- No-fee earning rate: 1.5x on travel and dining
- Annual-fee card: higher travel/dining rate, but the exact rate is not in the information I have
- Annual-fee card: two lounge passes
- Previously redeemed $218 in points: excluded, because it is a one-time historical value rather than a recurring annual benefit

Net annual cost before valuing points or lounge access

Option                         Fee       Credit       Net annual cost
Annual-fee card, credit used   $150      −$75         $75
Annual-fee card, no credit     $150      $0           $150
No-fee card                    $0        $0           $0

Therefore, the annual-fee card has an incremental annual cost of:

- $75 if the full travel credit is used
- $150 if the credit is not used

Break-even value per extra point

Let:

- L = your value for the two lounge passes
- B = any other quantifiable incremental value from the annual-fee card
- S = annual travel/dining spending receiving the higher rate
- r = annual-fee card’s earning rate
- The no-fee card’s rate = 1.5x

The annual-fee card’s extra points are:

(r − 1.5) × S

With the full $75 credit:

Break-even value per extra point =
($75 − L − B) ÷ [(r − 1.5) × S]

Without using the credit:

Break-even value per extra point =
($150 − L − B) ÷ [(r − 1.5) × S]

If lounge passes and other benefits are assigned no value, the hurdle is simply:

$75 ÷ extra points, if the credit is used

or

$150 ÷ extra points, if it is not used

Illustrations, assuming no value assigned to lounges or other benefits:

Premium rate    Eligible spend    Extra points    Value needed per extra point
2x              $5,000             2,500           3.00 cents
2x              $10,000            5,000           1.50 cents
3x              $5,000             7,500           1.00 cent
3x              $10,000            15,000          0.50 cents

Those examples are conditional because the premium card’s exact rate is not recorded here. The correct spending base is only the travel/dining spending for which the premium card earns more than 1.5x.

For example, if the two lounge passes are worth $30 total and the full credit is used, the extra-points hurdle falls from $75 to $45. At $5,000 of eligible spending:

- At 2x versus 1.5x: $45 ÷ 2,500 = 1.8 cents per extra point
- At 3x versus 1.5x: $45 ÷ 7,500 = 0.6 cents per extra point

Nonquantified tradeoffs

Annual-fee card advantages:

- Lounge access convenience, particularly during delays or long connections
- Travel protections, potentially including trip cancellation/interruption, delay, baggage, and rental-car coverage
- Purchase protections, extended warranty, return protection, or cellphone coverage
- Potentially better transfer partners, redemption flexibility, or rewards-related features
- Possible concierge, hotel, or other card-linked services
- Retaining the option to use premium benefits without buying separate lounge access or coverage

No-fee card advantages:

- No fixed annual cost and no need to manufacture spending to use a credit
- Simpler economics and less risk that a benefit expires unused
- Existing points remain preserved under the recorded product-change terms
- Lower exposure to changes in lounge availability, eligibility, capacity, or guest rules
- Less dependence on travel volume or on transactions qualifying under narrow credit rules
- Potentially simpler account management and fewer benefit terms to monitor

Operational or uncertain tradeoffs to verify separately:

- Whether the higher-rate card’s travel and dining categories exclude transit, rideshare, third-party bookings, or particular merchants
- Lounge network, guest access, capacity restrictions, expiration, and whether unused passes disappear immediately on conversion
- Whether travel protections apply only when the trip is paid for with that card
- Whether the product change preserves the account number, credit line, account age, autopay arrangements, digital-wallet tokens, and authorized users
- Any difference in foreign-transaction fees, APR, balance-transfer terms, or redemption restrictions
- Whether the annual fee is charged upfront while the credit posts later, creating a cash-flow difference
- Whether changing products can be reversed later
- Whether the issuer changes transfer partners, point expiration rules, redemption rates, or reward eligibility

The clean quantitative threshold is therefore $75 of incremental annual value when the credit is fully used, or $150 when it is not. The extra points must make up whatever remains after assigning values to the lounge passes and any other incremental benefits.

Comparison with the no-fee product change

The no-fee card:

- Removes the $75 travel credit and lounge passes

Compared with the no-fee card, the annual-fee card must provide at least $75 of additional annual value to justify keeping it:

$150 fee − $75 travel credit = $75 required incremental value

That $75 must come from some combination of:

- The two lounge passes

Practical decision rule:

Issuer terms to verify before choosing

1. Fee timing and refund
   - Exact annual-fee posting date.
   - Whether the fee is refundable after a product change.
   - The issuer’s downgrade/refund window—often expressed as a number of days after posting.
   - Whether the refund is full, prorated, or unavailable after that window.
   - Whether the fee can be waived or offset with a retention offer.

2. Product-change mechanics
   - Whether this is a true product change rather than a new account.
   - Whether the account number, credit line, account age, and payment history remain intact.
   - Whether there is a hard credit inquiry.
   - Whether autopay, recurring charges, digital-wallet tokens, and authorized users carry over.
   - Whether the change can be reversed later.

3. Points
   - Whether the existing points remain intact immediately after the change.
   - Whether points must be redeemed or transferred first.
   - Whether the points balance, transfer partners, redemption rates, or expiration rules change.
   - Whether any points or rewards can be clawed back because of the downgrade.

4. No-fee card rewards
   - Exact definition of “1.5x travel/dining.”
   - Whether travel includes transit, rideshare, hotels, rental cars, and third-party booking sites.
   - Whether there are caps, exclusions, rotating categories, or redemption restrictions.
   - The actual redemption value and whether travel redemptions require an issuer portal.
   - Foreign-transaction fees.

5. $75 travel credit
   - Eligible merchants and transaction types.
   - Whether it is based on a calendar year, cardmember year, or statement year.
   - Whether enrollment is required.
   - Whether credits are automatic and how long they take to post.
   - Whether unused credit expires.
   - What happens if a qualifying purchase is refunded or partially refunded.

6. Lounge passes
   - Which lounges and networks accept them.
   - Whether each pass covers only the cardholder or also a guest.
   - Whether taxes, reservations, or capacity restrictions apply.
   - Expiration dates and whether unused passes are forfeited after a product change.
   - Whether access depends on holding the original card on the date of entry.

7. Benefits lost on downgrade
   - Trip cancellation/interruption and delay coverage.
   - Rental-car coverage.
   - Baggage protection.
   - Purchase protection, return protection, and extended warranty.
   - Cellphone protection, concierge, hotel status, or other card-linked benefits.
   - Whether benefits remain available for purchases made before the product change.

8. Account and credit consequences
   - Any change to APR, minimum payment, credit-line terms, or penalty fees.
   - Whether the no-fee product has a different balance-transfer or cash-advance schedule.
   - Whether the issuer will close the account instead of converting it.
   - Whether a separate application is required.

The key number to get from the issuer is the downgrade deadline relative to the $150 fee posting. If the issuer confirms that you can product-change and receive a full fee refund, waiting until the fee posts may preserve flexibility—but only if the issuer confirms that sequence in writing.

Here is the issuer's secure-message transcript:

Product change to the no-fee card may be completed through April 14 to avoid the $150 annual fee. If the fee posts April 15, a product change completed within 30 days produces a full fee credit. Existing points remain in the same rewards account and pending rewards post normally. The $75 travel credit and lounge passes end immediately when the product change is processed.

Using the terms previously recorded:

- Annual-fee card: $150 annual fee
- Travel credit: $75, if fully usable
- No-fee card: $0 annual fee
- No-fee earning rate: 1.5x on travel and dining
- Annual-fee card: higher travel/dining rate, but the exact rate is not in the information I have
- Annual-fee card: two lounge passes
- Previously redeemed $218 in points: excluded, because it is a one-time historical value rather than a recurring annual benefit

Net annual cost before valuing points or lounge access

Option                         Fee       Credit       Net annual cost
Annual-fee card, credit used   $150      −$75         $75
Annual-fee card, no credit     $150      $0           $150
No-fee card                    $0        $0           $0

Therefore, the annual-fee card has an incremental annual cost of:

- $75 if the full travel credit is used
- $150 if the credit is not used

Break-even value per extra point

Let:

- L = your value for the two lounge passes
- B = any other quantifiable incremental value from the annual-fee card
- S = annual travel/dining spending receiving the higher rate
- r = annual-fee card’s earning rate
- The no-fee card’s rate = 1.5x

The annual-fee card’s extra points are:

(r − 1.5) × S

With the full $75 credit:

Break-even value per extra point =
($75 − L − B) ÷ [(r − 1.5) × S]

Without using the credit:

Break-even value per extra point =
($150 − L − B) ÷ [(r − 1.5) × S]

If lounge passes and other benefits are assigned no value, the hurdle is simply:

$75 ÷ extra points, if the credit is used

or

$150 ÷ extra points, if it is not used

Illustrations, assuming no value assigned to lounges or other benefits:

Premium rate    Eligible spend    Extra points    Value needed per extra point
2x              $5,000             2,500           3.00 cents
2x              $10,000            5,000           1.50 cents
3x              $5,000             7,500           1.00 cent
3x              $10,000            15,000          0.50 cents

Those examples are conditional because the premium card’s exact rate is not recorded here. The correct spending base is only the travel/dining spending for which the premium card earns more than 1.5x.

For example, if the two lounge passes are worth $30 total and the full credit is used, the extra-points hurdle falls from $75 to $45. At $5,000 of eligible spending:

- At 2x versus 1.5x: $45 ÷ 2,500 = 1.8 cents per extra point
- At 3x versus 1.5x: $45 ÷ 7,500 = 0.6 cents per extra point

Nonquantified tradeoffs

Annual-fee card advantages:

- Lounge access convenience, particularly during delays or long connections
- Travel protections, potentially including trip cancellation/interruption, delay, baggage, and rental-car coverage
- Purchase protections, extended warranty, return protection, or cellphone coverage
- Potentially better transfer partners, redemption flexibility, or rewards-related features
- Possible concierge, hotel, or other card-linked services
- Retaining the option to use premium benefits without buying separate lounge access or coverage

No-fee card advantages:

- No fixed annual cost and no need to manufacture spending to use a credit
- Simpler economics and less risk that a benefit expires unused
- Existing points remain preserved under the recorded product-change terms
- Lower exposure to changes in lounge availability, eligibility, capacity, or guest rules
- Less dependence on travel volume or on transactions qualifying under narrow credit rules
- Potentially simpler account management and fewer benefit terms to monitor

Operational or uncertain tradeoffs to verify separately:

- Whether the higher-rate card’s travel and dining categories exclude transit, rideshare, third-party bookings, or particular merchants
- Lounge network, guest access, capacity restrictions, expiration, and whether unused passes disappear immediately on conversion
- Whether travel protections apply only when the trip is paid for with that card
- Whether the product change preserves the account number, credit line, account age, autopay arrangements, digital-wallet tokens, and authorized users
- Any difference in foreign-transaction fees, APR, balance-transfer terms, or redemption restrictions
- Whether the annual fee is charged upfront while the credit posts later, creating a cash-flow difference
- Whether changing products can be reversed later
- Whether the issuer changes transfer partners, point expiration rules, redemption rates, or reward eligibility

The clean quantitative threshold is therefore $75 of incremental annual value when the credit is fully used, or $150 when it is not. The extra points must make up whatever remains after assigning values to the lounge passes and any other incremental benefits.

The two lounge passes are the main remaining value question. If their combined value is L, the known annual value is:

- $75 travel credit + L lounge value

Ignoring rewards and other benefits, the card breaks even only if the two lounge passes are worth at least $75 total, or $37.50 each. Any value from rewards, insurance, or other protections reduces that required lounge-pass value.

Comparison with the no-fee product change

The no-fee card:

- Preserves the points already earned
- Removes the $150 annual fee
- Removes the $75 travel credit and lounge passes
- Earns 1.5x on travel and dining, subject to the issuer’s exact terms

Compared with the no-fee card, the annual-fee card must provide at least $75 of additional annual value to justify keeping it:

$150 fee − $75 travel credit = $75 required incremental value

That $75 must come from some combination of:

- The two lounge passes
- Better rewards than the no-fee card
- Travel protections or purchase protections that the product change would remove
- Any other benefits you would actually use

Practical decision rule:

- Keep the $150 card if the lounge passes plus incremental rewards and protections are reliably worth at least $75 more than the no-fee card.
- Product-change to the no-fee card if you would not otherwise pay about $75 for the two lounge visits and the annual-fee card’s extra rewards or protections do not make up the difference.
- Do not count the already-redeemed $218 in points as future annual value.

Issuer terms to verify before choosing

1. Fee timing and refund
   - Exact annual-fee posting date.
   - Whether the fee is refundable after a product change.
   - The issuer’s downgrade/refund window—often expressed as a number of days after posting.
   - Whether the refund is full, prorated, or unavailable after that window.
   - Whether the fee can be waived or offset with a retention offer.

2. Product-change mechanics
   - Whether this is a true product change rather than a new account.
   - Whether the account number, credit line, account age, and payment history remain intact.
   - Whether there is a hard credit inquiry.
   - Whether autopay, recurring charges, digital-wallet tokens, and authorized users carry over.
   - Whether the change can be reversed later.

3. Points
   - Whether the existing points remain intact immediately after the change.
   - Whether points must be redeemed or transferred first.
   - Whether the points balance, transfer partners, redemption rates, or expiration rules change.
   - Whether any points or rewards can be clawed back because of the downgrade.

4. No-fee card rewards
   - Exact definition of “1.5x travel/dining.”
   - Whether travel includes transit, rideshare, hotels, rental cars, and third-party booking sites.
   - Whether there are caps, exclusions, rotating categories, or redemption restrictions.
   - The actual redemption value and whether travel redemptions require an issuer portal.
   - Foreign-transaction fees.

5. $75 travel credit
   - Eligible merchants and transaction types.
   - Whether it is based on a calendar year, cardmember year, or statement year.
   - Whether enrollment is required.
   - Whether credits are automatic and how long they take to post.
   - Whether unused credit expires.
   - What happens if a qualifying purchase is refunded or partially refunded.

6. Lounge passes
   - Which lounges and networks accept them.
   - Whether each pass covers only the cardholder or also a guest.
   - Whether taxes, reservations, or capacity restrictions apply.
   - Expiration dates and whether unused passes are forfeited after a product change.
   - Whether access depends on holding the original card on the date of entry.

7. Benefits lost on downgrade
   - Trip cancellation/interruption and delay coverage.
   - Rental-car coverage.
   - Baggage protection.
   - Purchase protection, return protection, and extended warranty.
   - Cellphone protection, concierge, hotel status, or other card-linked benefits.
   - Whether benefits remain available for purchases made before the product change.

8. Account and credit consequences
   - Any change to APR, minimum payment, credit-line terms, or penalty fees.
   - Whether the no-fee product has a different balance-transfer or cash-advance schedule.
   - Whether the issuer will close the account instead of converting it.
   - Whether a separate application is required.

The key number to get from the issuer is the downgrade deadline relative to the $150 fee posting. If the issuer confirms that you can product-change and receive a full fee refund, waiting until the fee posts may preserve flexibility—but only if the issuer confirms that sequence in writing.

Purpose and scope
This record preserves the original design intent for the expansion-nudge experiment. It is explicitly a historical, pre-launch plan and must not be confused with the experiment's later runtime state, readout, rollback, or any subsequent Expansion Assist work.

observed.body:
Historical design record — ORIGINAL PRE-LAUNCH PLAN

Date recorded: 2028-01-01

Purpose and scope
This record preserves the original design intent for the expansion-nudge experiment. It is explicitly a historical, pre-launch plan and must not be confused with the experiment's later runtime state, readout, rollback, or any subsequent Expansion Assist work.

Experiment identifier
- EXP-2023-05-expansion-nudge

Initial rollout
- 25% initial flag rollout.
- The rollout was intentionally narrow to avoid a large exposure before validating copy and placement.

Cohort scope
- Retained mid-segment accounts only.
- v2 accounts.
- 75–200 paid seats.
- Treatment: an in-product usage-panel prompt at day 60.

Feature flag
- expansion_nudge_60d_v1

Intended powered window
- Two weeks, contingent on the power calculation holding (“2 weeks if the power math holds”).

Original hypothesis / intended read
- Measure expansion MRR per account.
- Target at least +$8 expansion MRR per account over the intended two-week window.

Historical-status boundary
This entry records the original pre-launch design only. It does not assert that the flag is currently active, that the experiment later succeeded, or that the original plan became a blanket rollout. Later operation and outcomes are separate historical facts: the experiment was subsequently read as inconclusive, and the old day-60 flag was later retired/rolled back. Expansion Assist is a separate, behavior-based exploratory follow-on and is not this experiment.

Evidence

The attached Mixpanel screenshots are included as documentation of the observed cohort curves and the definition change. They are not intended to support a stronger conclusion than the underlying data allows.

Interpretation guardrail

Questions or requests for additional cuts—including Marcus’s—should be treated as questions, not as evidence that the result is positive, negative, urgent, or already understood. The next step is continued monitoring against the same definitions and maturity rules.

input.title: Historical framing note — Mid-segment churn investigation (Feb–Apr 2023)
input.body:
This investigation began in February 2023 when mid-segment monthly churn reached 5.1% on the then-standard 50–200-seat cut, versus a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline. The initial signal was validated independently rather than dismissed as a query or cohort artifact, and the team tested the main competing explanations in sequence. The pricing-page hypothesis was ruled out: churn was effectively flat across Entry, Standard, and Plus (5.0%, 5.2%, and 5.1%), while historical same-window comparisons did not show a recurring seasonal spike.

The investigation also clarified the measurement itself. Accounts in the 50–75-seat band were contaminating the mid-segment read, so the canonical definition became v2: 75–200 paid seats; the legacy 50–200 cut remains available only for historical comparison. Under the cleaner framing, the post–April 10 onboarding-trigger v2 improvement held despite a short April 17–20 wobble, and the April 30 validated read was 3.8% monthly churn. The completed work therefore established both a substantive recovery and a durable investigation practice: state the metric, cohort, window, hypothesis stack, effect size, and decision boundary explicitly, without treating a definition change as proof of improvement or a single noisy week as a new trend.

input.body:
Do not reuse the stale v1 cohort logic for new reads.

Corrected cohort boundary: mid-segment v2 is paid accounts with 75–200 seats, inclusive. The historical 50–200-seat v1 cut is retained only for comparison; 50–75-seat accounts belong outside the current mid-segment cohort.

Why the April read was noisy:
- Classification issue: the segment job incorrectly classified some 50–75-seat accounts as mid-segment, so the denominator was wrong before retention was calculated.
- Timing issue: the onboarding send read stale cohort membership from the cache window. Separately, the CS auto-onboarding-nudge outage delayed activation for affected accounts, shifting event timing and making the Apr 17 dip look noisier than the underlying result.

Use the 75–200-seat paid-account definition, refreshed membership, and matched maturity/timing rules for future analysis.

Corrected cohort boundary: mid-segment v2 is paid accounts with 75–200 seats, inclusive. The historical 50–200-seat v1 cut is retained only for comparison; 50–75-seat accounts belong outside the current mid-segment cohort.

Why the April read was noisy:
- Classification issue: the segment job incorrectly classified some 50–75-seat accounts as mid-segment, so the denominator was wrong before retention was calculated.
- Timing issue: the onboarding send read stale cohort membership from the cache window. Separately, the CS auto-onboarding-nudge outage delayed activation for affected accounts, shifting event timing and making the Apr 17 dip look noisier than the underlying result.

Use the 75–200-seat paid-account definition, refreshed membership, and matched maturity/timing rules for future analysis.

checks.reason: The title identifies this as the “April 2023 onboarding and mid-segment analysis — data-quality erratum.” The body sets the corrected boundary as “paid accounts with 75–200 seats, inclusive,” excludes 50–75-seat accounts from the current cohort, and explains both sources of noise: “the segment job incorrectly classified some 50–75-seat accounts as mid-segment, so the denominator was wrong” and “the onboarding send read stale cohort membership from the cache window,” which added timing noise.

Here’s a deliberately boring version you can drop into the doc:

April 27 update

`lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2` reached 100% rollout on April 10. The first post-ship cohort was directionally positive, followed by a small wobble in the next read. That wobble was not treated as evidence of either a regression or a definitive win; we checked cohort composition, instrumentation, and the underlying segment definitions first. Subsequent data is settling back into the expected range.

The current read is “promising and still being monitored,” not “proven” or “fixed.” One clean week is not enough to establish a durable effect.

Cohort definition

For the current operational read, mid-segment is defined as 75–200 seats. The prior 50–200-seat bucket combined materially different behavior, particularly in the 50–75-seat range, and made the trend harder to interpret. Historical v1 cuts may remain available for continuity, but new reporting should use the 75–200 definition and show the 50–75 range separately where useful.

Evidence

The attached Mixpanel screenshots are included as documentation of the observed cohort curves and the definition change. They are not intended to support a stronger conclusion than the underlying data allows.

Interpretation guardrail

Questions or requests for additional cuts—including Marcus’s—should be treated as questions, not as evidence that the result is positive, negative, urgent, or already understood. The next step is continued monitoring against the same definitions and maturity rules.

input.title: Helio lifecycle design lineage — onboarding trigger vs. activation metric
input.body:
Design lineage note — 2028-01-01

These are two related but separate design threads. The onboarding-email trigger change was a lifecycle-delivery change; the activation-definition review was a measurement change. Do not document them as one combined change.

1. Onboarding email trigger change
The original onboarding touch was scheduled on fixed calendar day 7. For the targeted mid-segment cohort (50–200 seats) that had not activated by day 7, the design moved toward activation-state-based timing: suppress the fixed day-7 touch and send the onboarding touch from the activation-triggered path instead. The guardrails were narrow: leave already-activated users, controls, users outside the segment, other lifecycle touches, and activation-triggered sends outside the suppression rule unchanged; also protect against late-activation duplicate sends. The successor implementation is recorded as Activation-triggered onboarding touch v2; the old day-7 trigger variant is decommissioned.

2. Why activation was reviewed, and the successor direction
Separately, activation definition v2 was reviewed because its “first integration plus two logins within 14 days” gate was too UI-shaped: it could miss accounts that completed a real integration and had data flowing but did not click around twice. The intended successor direction was activation definition v3: measure product proof through a completed first integration plus at least one meaningful in-product/product-seen event within 14 days, replacing the two-login gate. The exact qualifying event still required final lock before treating v3 as final, with historical backfill and dashboard-definition updates planned.

Lineage boundary
The first thread changes when and to whom a lifecycle email is delivered. The second changes how activation is defined and measured. The trigger change did not itself redefine activation, and the metric review did not itself change the email scheduler.

input.title: Archive Note — April 17, 2023: Second Post-Ship Cohort Dip
input.body:
Archive date: April 17, 2023

The second post-ship cohort showed a temporary dip to +1.4 points in week-one retention versus baseline, below the first post-ship cohort’s +3.2-point read and the pooled experiment result of +3.1 points. The dip was a one-time measurement artifact caused by an upstream CS auto-onboarding-nudge outage. While that nudge path was unavailable, affected mid-segment accounts activated later than expected, shifting the timing of the relevant events represented in the cohort. The downstream activation-event email still sent, but at a different point in the onboarding flow.

The outage lasted approximately 36 hours. This note intentionally records the duration without recording an exact outage start or end date.

After the incident, the CS auto-onboarding-nudge system was back up. The 100%-rolled-out lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2 remained operational, and its conversion logic was not implicated. The cohort dip therefore reflected shifted activation timing rather than a regression in the onboarding-trigger experiment. Subsequent monitoring showed the system and lifecycle behavior returning to a clean, normal condition; no broader churn or activation failure was identified.

input.title: July 2023 decision rights — Helio Start and retained-mid expansion
input.body:
Period-specific historical record — July 2023 only. This note is for governance retrospective use and is not current org policy.

Scope
Two workstreams were deliberately kept separate: Helio Start, an internal operating-model pre-discovery effort for a sub-50-seat self-serve motion; and retained-mid expansion, then carried forward as the behavior-based Expansion Assist exploration. They had separate evidence, decision language, and readouts, with no blended totals or cross-workstream proof.

Strategic decision lane
- Riley held the decision rules, executive tradeoffs, and cross-functional guardrails for both lanes.
- For Helio Start, the strategic decision was to remain in guarded pre-discovery through July—not to treat the work as a launch path, Q3 revenue commitment, or automatic August beta. Any later beta discussion depended on clearing eligibility, instrumentation, lifecycle, and support gates.
- For retained-mid expansion, the strategic decision was that the expansion nudge was not evidence for Helio Start and did not justify a blanket retained-mid rollout or forecast credit. The next step was a narrower, behavior-based Expansion Assist exploration.
- Priya’s role was to set and review the July operating split; the reused investigation framework was informal and not a permanent org chart or formal company process.

Routine execution lane
- Owen owned the first-pass readout shapes: Helio Start baseline and field-completeness cuts, plus retained-mid expansion eligibility and measurement cuts, with samples, caveats, denominators, and unusable evidence called out.
- Ines owned lifecycle-fork risk mapping and copy boundaries for both workstreams. Routine lifecycle or copy work could proceed only within the agreed boundaries; state-changing work remained out of scope until the relevant gates cleared.
- Routine execution produced evidence and options; it did not change eligibility, authorize a launch or rollout, create forecast or revenue credit, or merge the two workstreams.

Retrospective boundary
These rights and assignments describe the July 2023 working arrangement. They should not be read as a standing ownership model, current approval policy, or current org chart.

  A required field was stale, unresolved, or conflicting at decision time, or the recorded freshness limit was crossed. The affected field remains held and fails closed until a fresh source check and ordinary reevaluation occur.

Breach:
  The source crossed its recorded freshness limit before restoration or reevaluation. Record the resulting field-specific holds and any customer-impact controls. Never describe a breach as merely an alert.

Customer Success should receive these answers:

1. “If authority is verified, does that also mean outreach is allowed?”
   
   No. Verified external-system authority means the connector is ready for the required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action. It is not contact permission by itself. Outreach may proceed only when the specific evaluated decision has all required current state, including active entitlement, connector authentication, a qualifying human admin, no active Customer Success adoption or renewal work, and any applicable messaging approval.

2. “Can a proceed result clear a hold in another workspace for the same person?”

   No. Proceed is scoped to the evaluated workspace and decision. It does not manually release or clear a hold elsewhere, even for the same person. The other workspace must be evaluated using its own current state and receive a fresh check. A held field may constrain dependent messages, but a proceed result cannot propagate clearance across workspaces.

Breach:

input.title: CS auto-nudge — first-live control-evidence scorecard
input.body:
CONTROL-EVIDENCE SCORECARD

Status: CLOSED first-live review evidence
Coverage: May 8–June 13, 2025
Scope: CS auto-nudge production decisions on the shared-state path
Evidence lane: system-control performance only; not customer-outcome, conversion, revenue, forecast, or mature-reliability evidence

1. DENOMINATOR AND RECONCILIATION — PASS

Primary denominator: 1,184 unique evaluated decisions

Decision-level reconciliation:
- Failed closed at decision time: 53
- Proceeded or suppressed using current state: 1,131
- Reconciliation: 53 + 1,131 = 1,184
- Unclassified or unmatched decisions: 0 reported
- Counting rule: one primary ledger row per scheduled decision; holds, fresh checks, and reevaluations are linked audit history, not additional decisions

Control interpretation:
- Failed closed means stale or conflicting required state blocked the decision; it is distinct from a final current-state suppression or proceed.
- Current-state handling means the decision ultimately proceeded or was suppressed after evaluation of current supported state.
- Do not add intermediate hold events to the denominator or present intermediate and final outcomes as additive populations.

2. FAILED-CLOSED DECISIONS — 53 TOTAL

Control result: PASS — stale/conflicting required state failed closed; no manual release from stale state.

Recorded hold population:
- Stale or conflicting required-state decisions: 53
- May 20 Customer Success-work freshness-delay subset: 12
- Other failed-closed decisions outside that delayed-source subset: 41
- Final field-by-field split for the remaining 41: not asserted in the locked first-live evidence; retain the row-level hold reason and source history for audit rather than infer a breakdown.

Required handling:
- A stale, unresolved, or conflicting required field remains held until the source is checked and the system reevaluates through the ordinary path.
- A hold is a control outcome, not a delivery failure and not permission to reuse an earlier result.

3. CURRENT-STATE DECISIONS — 1,131 TOTAL

Control result: recorded final disposition population
- Proceeded or suppressed using current state: 1,131
- This population is the complement of the 53 decision-time fail-closed rows in the primary denominator.
- A current-state suppression reflects active Customer Success adoption or renewal work; it is not a failed-closed decision.
- A proceed result is scoped to the evaluated workspace and decision and is not portable approval for another workspace, consumer, or message.

4. DELAYED-SOURCE SUBSET — COUNT ONCE ONLY

Event: May 20 Customer Success source refresh delay
Affected unique scheduled decisions: 12
Initial control action: all 12 failed closed when the active-Customer-Success-work field crossed its freshness limit; the prior no-work value was not reused.
Fresh-check disposition on the same 12 rows:
- Valid suppressions after refresh: 8
- Proceeds after refresh: 4
- Total fresh reevaluations: 12
- Stale-state nudges released: 0
- Manual releases: 0
- Customer corrections: 0
- Rollback required: 0

Counting treatment:
- The 12 rows are included once in the 1,184 primary denominator and once within the 53 failed-closed decision-time rows.
- The later 8 suppressions and 4 proceeds are final dispositions linked to those same 12 rows; they are not added to 1,184.
- The source-delay event, initial holds, fresh checks, timestamps, and final outcomes remain linked audit history.

5. CROSS-SURFACE AGREEMENT — PASS

Compared views: reporting, lifecycle, and decision/operator views
Governed fields checked:
- External-system authority
- Connector authentication
- Entitlement
- Qualifying-human-admin status
- Active Customer Success adoption or renewal work

Result:
- Decisions with a governed-field status difference across corresponding reporting and lifecycle views: 0 reported
- Adjacent lifecycle messages that assumed eligibility: none reported
- Messaging-state alignment: confirmed
- Shared-state consumer and field-specific operator view: healthy and coordinated

Evidence boundary:
- This supports the statement that no evaluated decision carried a different governed-field status across the corresponding views.
- It does not support the claim “zero decision errors.”

6. CUSTOMER-CORRECTION AND SAFETY OUTCOMES — PASS

- Customer corrections required: 0
- Stale-state nudges sent: 0 reported for the delayed-source event
- Incident stop: none reported
- Manual override: none reported
- Rollback use: none reported; coordinated rollback remained available

7. EXTERNAL-SYSTEM AUTHORITY — NARROW DEFINITION

Definition used in this scorecard:
External-system authority means verified readiness for the selected connector’s required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action. It is a connector-readiness state only.

Explicit exclusions:
- It is not consent.
- It is not message eligibility.
- It is not blanket or automated-contact permission.
- It is not permission to contact a customer, release a nudge, clear a hold, or authorize another lifecycle message.
- Connector authentication and external-system authority remain separate governed fields.

A customer-facing or lifecycle message still requires its own applicable messaging rules and a fresh current-state evaluation, including active entitlement, connector authentication, qualifying human-admin status, no active Customer Success adoption or renewal work, and all other required governed conditions.

8. CONTROL OWNERSHIP AND EVIDENCE BOUNDARIES

- Owen: routine operating explanation, unique-decision denominator, and exception ledger.
- Ines: messaging-state alignment and routine messaging-state review.
- Daniela: engineering release, production health, and coordinated rollback control.
- Riley: disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, customer-correction decisions, incident stops, and executive claims.

Decision-use boundary:
- This is a closed first-live control-evidence scorecard for May 8–June 13, 2025.
- It is not a mature-result declaration.
- It does not grant authority to another consumer, expand the governed scope, or authorize customer contact.
- Evidence supports system-control performance only.

9. AUDIT TRACE

- Locked June 12 pre-read: 1,184 unique scheduled decisions; 53 failed closed; 1,131 current-state proceeds/suppressions; 12 May 20 delayed-source rows; no cross-view differences; no customer correction; messaging alignment and rollback readiness recorded. Source record: riley-003009-user, June 12, 2025.
- May 20 delay and fresh-check record: same 12 rows; 8 suppressions; 4 proceeds; no stale-state nudge, manual release, correction, or rollback. Source record: riley-002959-user, May 20, 2025.
- Formal close: 1,184 unique evaluated decisions; 53 stale/conflicting fail-closed; 1,131 current-state proceeds/suppressions; no governed-field status difference; no customer correction. Source record: riley-003012-user, June 13, 2025.
- Authority-language control: connector readiness for owner-level permission or network-allowlist action, not automated-contact permission. Source record: riley-003010-user, June 13, 2025.

results.content:
Here’s the plain-language reading:

- The $615 deductible is the amount Mom may have to pay for covered prescription drugs during 2027 before the plan begins using the stated post-deductible prices.
- For Ventolin HFA, the notice gives a $49 preferred-pharmacy copay after that deductible is satisfied. It does not tell us the exact amount she would pay for Ventolin before reaching $615.
- The deductible is cumulative for the year. Spending on other deductible-eligible medicines can help reach it; Mom does not necessarily have to spend $615 on Ventolin alone.
- “Preferred pharmacy” means the $49 figure applies only when the prescription is filled at a pharmacy the plan lists as preferred and for the exact covered prescription and quantity.

Simple examples:

1. Before the deductible is met:
   If Mom has not yet reached $615 and fills Ventolin, the plan might charge her the drug’s negotiated cost—or another amount specified in the plan—instead of $49. The notice alone does not tell us what that pre-deductible price is. Any amount that the plan counts as deductible spending would reduce the remaining deductible.

2. After the deductible is met:
   Once Mom has accumulated $615 in applicable covered drug spending, a later Ventolin fill at a preferred pharmacy could cost $49, assuming the prescription and quantity match the notice.

3. Near the deductible:
   If Mom has already accumulated $500 and then fills Ventolin, she has $115 left before reaching the deductible. The exact amount charged for that fill, and how the claim is split if it crosses the deductible, must be confirmed with the plan. After the deductible is met, later qualifying Ventolin fills would be expected to use the $49 copay.

4. The two tier 1 generics:
   Their listed $0 preferred-pharmacy copays mean Mom would owe $0 at a preferred pharmacy under the stated cost-sharing rule. That suggests those generics may bypass the deductible, unlike Ventolin, but the notice wording should be confirmed.

One precise question to ask the plan:

“For Mom’s exact Ventolin HFA strength and quantity, does the $615 deductible apply to that prescription but not to the two tier 1 generics—so that she pays the plan’s specified pre-deductible amount for Ventolin until $615 is met, then pays $49 per fill at a preferred pharmacy, while the generics remain $0 from the first fill?”

results.content:
What the notice confirms

- The plan intends to charge $28.90 per month beginning January 1, 2025, compared with $14.20 in 2024.
- If Mom actually pays those amounts for all 12 months, the premium portion would be:
  - 2024: $170.40
  - 2025: $346.80
  - Increase: $176.40 per year, or $14.70 per month
- The plan’s stated annual drug deductible will be $590, compared with $545 in 2024—an increase of $45.
- The preferred-pharmacy network will change, so her current pharmacy cannot be assumed to remain preferred.
- An Annual Notice of Change is intended to describe plan changes taking effect in January.[1]

What the notice does not establish

- It does not establish Mom’s actual premium payment. The $28.90 may be changed by Extra Help, another subsidy, a late-enrollment penalty, an income-related adjustment, premium withholding, or a different billing arrangement. Extra Help can affect premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance.[7]
- It does not establish her total annual prescription cost. That depends on her specific drugs, strengths, quantities, fill frequency, coverage status, tiers, cost-sharing, pharmacy, and mail-order choices.
- It does not show what each drug will cost in 2025 or whether any drug has moved to a higher tier.
- It does not disclose prior authorization, step therapy, quantity limits, specialty-pharmacy requirements, or other utilization restrictions.
- The $45 deductible increase is not necessarily a $45 additional bill. If Mom’s covered drug spending is low, she may not reach either deductible. If she does reach the deductible, the difference may matter.
- It does not establish that her current pharmacy will have the same price. Preferred in-network pharmacies may offer lower cost-sharing than other in-network pharmacies, while out-of-network fills may cost substantially more.[3]
- It does not provide a personalized annual estimate. Separately, 2025 Part D has a $2,000 annual out-of-pocket threshold for covered Part D drugs.[6] That is not a prediction of Mom’s spending and is not a complete annual budget: premiums, non-covered drugs, and costs outside covered Part D benefits may be treated separately.

Document checklist

Obtain these documents for Mom’s current plan and each plan being considered:

[ ] Complete 2025 Annual Notice of Change, including attachments, plan name, contract/PBP number, and effective date.

[ ] 2025 Evidence of Coverage. This provides the detailed rules, covered benefits, cost-sharing, exceptions, and member obligations.[2]

[ ] 2025 Summary of Benefits or benefit chart, if available.

[ ] Final 2025 formulary. For every medication, record:
- Exact name, strength, dosage form, and quantity
- Tier
- Whether the deductible applies
- Copay or coinsurance before and after the deductible
- Prior authorization, step therapy, quantity limits, or specialty-pharmacy requirements

Medicare recommends checking the formulary before joining a plan.[4]

[ ] Complete 2025 Pharmacy Directory. Mark:
- Mom’s usual pharmacy
- A backup pharmacy
- Mail-order pharmacy
- Pharmacies near home and any regular travel locations
- Which locations are preferred and which are merely in-network

[ ] Premium billing notice or statement showing the gross premium, subsidies, penalties, adjustments, and actual payment method.

[ ] Any Extra Help/LIS, Medicaid, Medicare Savings Program, employer/union, VA, or state-assistance notices.

[ ] Mom’s complete medication list, including occasional prescriptions, insulin, specialty drugs, vaccines, and drugs obtained through a doctor’s office where relevant.

[ ] Last year’s pharmacy receipts and Explanation of Benefits statements, preferably covering a full 12 months.

[ ] A Medicare Plan Finder comparison using Mom’s ZIP code, exact medications, quantities, expected fills, and each pharmacy she might use. Medicare’s comparison tool supports using saved drugs and pharmacies.[5]

[ ] If this is Medicare Advantage rather than a standalone Part D plan, the plan’s 2025 health-coverage Evidence of Coverage and medical out-of-pocket limit as well.

Questions to ask each plan

1. “Is $28.90 the gross premium or Mom’s actual net premium? Does it include or exclude Extra Help, penalties, or income-related adjustments?”

2. “For each of Mom’s prescriptions, is it covered in 2025? What are the exact tier, deductible treatment, copay or coinsurance, and estimated 30-day and 90-day costs?”

3. “What would each prescription cost at her usual pharmacy, a preferred pharmacy, a non-preferred in-network pharmacy, and mail order?”

4. “Are any medications subject to prior authorization, step therapy, quantity limits, specialty-pharmacy rules, or required generic or biosimilar substitution?”

5. “Will any existing prior authorization or exception carry over into 2025? If not, what must her prescriber submit?”

6. “Does the $590 deductible apply to every medication? Are any drugs or categories treated differently?”

7. “Which pharmacies are preferred, and is Mom’s pharmacy confirmed as preferred in the effective 2025 directory?”

8. “Are any of her medications being removed, moved to a higher tier, or subjected to new restrictions?”

9. “Please provide a written estimate based on Mom’s exact medication list and pharmacy, showing annual premium plus expected drug costs.” Ask for both:
- An ordinary-use estimate
- A high-cost scenario

10. “Is Mom receiving or eligible for Extra Help, Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program, or state pharmaceutical assistance, and how would that change her actual 2025 costs?”

11. “Is the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan available, and which costs would remain outside it?” Treat this as a payment-scheduling option, not a discount.

12. “If Mom changes plans, when will coverage begin, and could the change affect retiree, employer, union, or other health coverage?” During the ordinary annual enrollment period, plan changes made October 15 through December 7 generally begin January 1.[5]

Use this comparison format

Plan | Net annual premium | Deductible | Annual cost for each drug | Preferred-pharmacy total | Mail-order total | Restrictions | Ordinary annual estimate | High-cost estimate

Use identical medications, quantities, fill frequency, pharmacy assumptions, and a 12-month period for every plan. The cheapest premium is not necessarily the cheapest plan overall.
