I can establish the prior Cherrywood baseline, but I can’t calculate the renewal increase exactly because the renewal declarations themselves aren’t available in the connected mailbox or conversation record. I checked the available inbox/archive, and both returned no messages.

Prior Cherrywood policy baseline

- Annualized premium: $24.60/month × 12 = $295.20
- Personal property: $30,000, replacement cost
- Personal liability: $300,000
- Deductible: $500
- Loss of use: $10,000
- Water backup: $5,000
- Cherrywood: listed as an interested party

The prior policy was selected in April for coverage beginning May 1, 2024.

Renewal calculation

Once you provide the renewal declarations’ total annual premium:

- Dollar increase = renewal premium − $295.20
- Percentage increase = dollar increase ÷ $295.20 × 100

Use the declarations-page annual premium rather than multiplying a displayed monthly amount. The earlier record contains a small inconsistency: the monthly figures imply an $81.60 annual difference between the two quotes, while the insurer’s stated difference was $84.

Coverage comparison

Compare the renewal against these exact fields:

| Coverage item | Prior Cherrywood policy | Renewal |
|---|---:|---:|
| Personal property | $30,000, replacement cost | Need declarations |
| Personal liability | $300,000 | Need declarations |
| Deductible | $500 | Need declarations |
| Loss of use | $10,000 | Need declarations |
| Water backup | $5,000 | Need declarations |
| Interested party | Cherrywood | Need declarations |
| Policy term/address | May 1, 2024 Cherrywood policy | Need declarations |

Interpretation:

- If all coverage fields are unchanged, the entire premium increase is a rate/pricing change, subject to any changed fees, discounts, rating factors, or billing charges.
- If limits increased, the increase is partly coverage-driven.
- If the deductible decreased, that generally represents richer coverage and could justify some increase.
- If replacement-cost coverage, water backup, or higher liability was removed, the premium increase would not be explained by broader coverage and should be questioned.
- Also check for changed discounts, claims history, occupancy/use classification, protection-device credits, pet or household information, installment fees, and any endorsement changes.

Please paste or upload the renewal declarations page—or just provide its annual premium and the six coverage fields—and I can produce the exact dollar increase, percentage increase, and a line-by-line rate-versus-coverage conclusion.

input.title: Cherrywood Watercolor Reset & Upkeep Guide — January 1, 2028
input.body:
Cherrywood watercolor reset & upkeep
January 1, 2028

Purpose
Keep the dedicated, naturally lit Cherrywood dining-corner setup ready for a quiet Sunday painting block without turning upkeep into another project.

Workspace and supplies
- Painting table in the dedicated dining corner, with the narrow supply cabinet nearby.
- Keep the table turned 90 degrees from the window so wet paper does not catch direct glare.
- Keep the plain matte white foam board on the shadow side, leaning slightly toward the work surface as a reflector.
- Supplies kept here: paints (including ultramarine blue, burnt sienna, quinacridone rose, phthalo blue, and yellow ochre), two rigid boards, two palettes, brushes, 9×12-inch 140-pound cold-press paper, masking tape, pencils, towels, and two water containers.
- Use a wet zone for water, rinsing, and active palettes; keep a separate dry zone for paper, boards, pencils, finished work, and the portfolio.

Initial reset — January 1 (15 minutes)
1. Clear the painting table and wipe the permanent surface with a clean, dry towel; keep the work surface protected by a towel before setting out materials.
2. Return both boards, both palettes, brushes, paper, tape, pencils, towels, and the two water containers to their established cabinet/table locations.
3. Check paint pans/tubes for secure lids and usable paint; arrange the usual colors together so the palette is ready without searching.
4. Make sure the 9×12 paper is clean, dry, and flat enough to tape to a board. Keep finished or drying sheets out of the wet zone and store fully dry work in the private watercolor portfolio.
5. Re-establish the light: table rotated away from the window, foam board opposite the window, and—when natural light is insufficient—the neutral-daylight LED task lamp positioned out of the direct line of sight and aimed to avoid glare on wet washes.

Per session — before painting
- Put a towel down first; assign one board/palette set and one water container to each painter when sharing the setup.
- Tape the 9×12 sheet to a board in the dry zone, then place the palette and one water container in the wet zone.
- Fill the water container, lay out only the paints and brushes likely to be used, and keep pencils/tape within reach but away from water.
- Check the paper from the side for glare before beginning; adjust the board, foam board, or lamp rather than judging a wet wash under reflected light.

Per session — after painting
- Leave finished sheets flat until fully dry; then place them in the private watercolor portfolio or return unused paper to the dry storage area.
- Rinse brushes thoroughly in the water container, reshape the tips, and leave them to dry flat or bristle-up—not soaking.
- Empty and rinse both water containers; wipe palettes clean enough that old pigment will not contaminate the next session.
- Remove masking tape slowly once the sheet is fully dry, wipe the table and boards with a towel, and return every supply to its cabinet/table home.

Weekly upkeep
- Do a five-minute reset after the weekly block: dust the table, cabinet top, boards, palettes, and lamp/foam-board edges with a dry towel.
- Inspect brushes for dried paint, splayed tips, or loose handles; set aside anything needing attention rather than putting it back in the ready set.
- Check the paper stack for dampness, buckling, bent corners, or depleted 9×12 sheets; keep paper flat and dry.
- Confirm that both water containers, towels, tape, pencils, and the core colors are still present and ready.
- Keep the wet and dry zones visibly separate so the corner can be started immediately next time.

Occasional upkeep
- Clean palette wells and the two boards more thoroughly when pigment buildup begins to affect color or the board surface becomes tacky.
- Wash and dry brushes individually when routine rinsing no longer removes pigment; never leave them standing in water.
- Re-sort the narrow cabinet when supplies migrate, keeping frequently used paints, paper, brushes, palettes, boards, tape, pencils, towels, and water containers together.
- Recheck the table orientation and foam-board position whenever the season or painting time changes. If using the task lamp, compare a color or value under neutral daylight before changing the painting itself.
- Review finished work periodically: only fully dry sheets go into the private portfolio; gently flatten a mildly buckled sheet only with the conservative no-heat method already used for the Cherrywood setup.

Ready-to-paint check
Table protected; light controlled; two boards and palettes present; brushes clean and usable; 9×12 paper dry and flat; paints secured; tape and pencils present; two water containers empty/clean; wet and dry zones clear.

input.title: Evidence Maturation Case Note: Onboarding Timing Analysis
input.body:
# Evidence Maturation Case Note: Onboarding Timing Analysis

## Stage 1 — Initial provisional cut

- **Population and split:** v1 mid-segment signups (50–200 seats), anchored on signup date, using the same January scan/Owen-check cohort logic. The comparison was whether users had activated before the exact calendar-day-7 onboarding email or were still unactivated when it arrived.
- **Observed churn:** approximately **3.1%** for users activated before day 7, versus approximately **7.8%** for users still unactivated at day 7 and receiving the touch pre-activation.
- **Evidence strength:** the direction was notable, but the sample was still described as flimsy and needed another week of observation. The groups were not randomly assigned: activation status precedes the send for some users and is related to underlying readiness or risk. The cohort cut therefore showed an association, not an estimate of the email’s causal effect.
- **Why it was not decision-ready:** the early sample could have been unstable, and the cut could not separate mistimed messaging from the fact that users who had not activated were already a higher-risk group. It was a hypothesis signal—not grounds to declare the day-7 email the cause of churn or to make a production change.

## Stage 2 — Sharpened read

- **Same definitions, stronger maturity:** the activation-day rerun preserved the same 50–200-seat mid-segment, signup anchor, and activated-before-touch versus post-day-7 pre-activation groups. The read reached **n=210**.
- **Observed churn:** **3.1%** for users activated before the onboarding touch versus **7.8%** for users still unactivated after day 7—a **4.7-point observed gap**, large enough to be difficult to dismiss as random wobble in this read.
- **Interpretation:** this was the first load-bearing, directional evidence that a state-blind, calendar-day-7 send may be arriving at the wrong moment for drifting mid-segment users. It materially strengthened the onboarding-timing hypothesis, but the cohort cut alone still did not establish that the email caused the churn difference.

## How the evidence informed the test

The sharpened read justified testing an **activation-state-aware journey**, rather than simply moving the email from day 7. The planned direction was to suppress only the fixed calendar-day-7 touch for treated mid-segment users who had not activated, preserve the existing touch for users activated before day 7, leave activation-triggered sends and controls unchanged, and keep the current calendar-day path as a holdout. The subsequent test—not the observational cohort cut—was the appropriate vehicle for estimating whether changing the timing improved retention.

input.title: Archive Note — Onboarding-Trigger Result at the May 12, 2023 Company All-Hands
input.body:
Archive note date: 2028-01-01
Event: Formal company all-hands, May 12, 2023
Presentation: “Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned”

Scope
This note records how the onboarding-trigger result was presented and credited in the May 12, 2023 company all-hands. It is an event-specific recognition record, not a universal rule for attribution or credit.

Audience and format
The presentation was delivered to the whole company audience of approximately 140 people. Riley Tanaka described the format as a full 15-minute talk followed by 10 minutes of Q&A. [1][2]

How the result was framed
The presentation was deliberately framed as a method-and-learning account rather than a “drama deck” or a postmortem of a problem already fixed. The sequence presented was:

- define the cohort cut;
- enumerate hypotheses;
- apply a rule-out cadence;
- run the onboarding-trigger A/B test; and
- wait for a stabilization cohort before treating the result as something known.

The planned deck also included the before/after seat-band comparison, the April 10 rollout break, and a short framework for what should be documented rather than left as tribal knowledge. The onboarding-trigger discussion therefore presented the result together with its evidentiary path and limits, including the later cohort redefinition from 50–200 to 75–200 seats. [1][2][3]

Result as presented
The contemporaneous experiment record identified EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger as a positive pooled read: week-1 retention was +3.1 percentage points for treatment versus control, p = 0.04, across n = 420 in two cohorts. The second cohort itself was reported at +3.4 percentage points, n = 200. The operational decision was to proceed toward the April 10 full rollout while retaining integrity and guardrail checks. [4][5]

The presentation’s framing emphasized that the team did not act on the first significant-looking read alone: it waited for the stabilization cohort and used the cohort cut, hypothesis enumeration, rule-outs, and A/B evidence as the chain supporting the result. This was presented as the lesson of this investigation and as a practice to use elsewhere—not as proof that the result generalized automatically to every cohort. [1][2]

Contributors explicitly credited in the all-hands presentation

Archive note date: 2028-01-01
Event: Formal company all-hands, May 12, 2023
Presentation: “Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned”

Scope
This note records how the onboarding-trigger result was presented and credited in the May 12, 2023 company all-hands. It is an event-specific recognition record, not a universal rule for attribution or credit.

Audience and format
The presentation was delivered to the whole company audience of approximately 140 people. Riley Tanaka described the format as a full 15-minute talk followed by 10 minutes of Q&A. [1][2]

How the result was framed
The presentation was deliberately framed as a method-and-learning account rather than a “drama deck” or a postmortem of a problem already fixed. The sequence presented was:

- define the cohort cut;
- enumerate hypotheses;
- apply a rule-out cadence;
- run the onboarding-trigger A/B test; and
- wait for a stabilization cohort before treating the result as something known.

The planned deck also included the before/after seat-band comparison, the April 10 rollout break, and a short framework for what should be documented rather than left as tribal knowledge. The onboarding-trigger discussion therefore presented the result together with its evidentiary path and limits, including the later cohort redefinition from 50–200 to 75–200 seats. [1][2][3]

Result as presented
The contemporaneous experiment record identified EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger as a positive pooled read: week-1 retention was +3.1 percentage points for treatment versus control, p = 0.04, across n = 420 in two cohorts. The second cohort itself was reported at +3.4 percentage points, n = 200. The operational decision was to proceed toward the April 10 full rollout while retaining integrity and guardrail checks. [4][5]

The presentation’s framing emphasized that the team did not act on the first significant-looking read alone: it waited for the stabilization cohort and used the cohort cut, hypothesis enumeration, rule-outs, and A/B evidence as the chain supporting the result. Prep notes

Core framing

This is not a pricing-only decision. It is a product, operations, support, and sales-boundary decision. The question is whether we can offer a repeatable sub-50-seat product without letting every small account become a bespoke 200-seat implementation.

Recommended boundary

Sub-50 means 49 paid seats or fewer. Keep 50–75 in the starter framing; do not blur it into the 75–200 mid-segment definition.

Supportable in a Q3 launch

- Fixed seat cap and fixed entitlements
- Standard plan and billing flow
- Standard workspace and permission model
- Standard onboarding path with documentation and lightweight assistance
- Standard support channel and response expectations
- Standard import path where the product already supports it
- Clear upgrade path when the account outgrows the tier
- Sales can sell only what is in the published package

Custom-small-account pain / refuse by default

- Custom invoicing or contract terms
- Migration or data-cleaning services
- Bespoke permissions or workspace limits
- Dedicated onboarding or implementation help
- SSO/SCIM, audit-log, or other enterprise controls unless already productized for this tier
- Exceptions that let a sub-50 account buy individual pieces of the 75–200/enterprise operating model
- Manual entitlement overrides
- Sales promises that require Product, Engineering, or Support to make a one-off commitment

The sentence to use

“We can support a sub-50 offer in Q3 only if it is a bounded, repeatable product. If the launch requires exceptions in entitlements, onboarding, billing, migration, or support, then Q3 is not real for that version.”

Decision needed in the room

Q3 should be a yes only if all four owners can commit to the standard path:

1. Product: entitlement and feature fences are explicit.
2. Engineering/operations: onboarding, billing, workspace, permissions, and import paths work without manual intervention.
3. Support: the support model and volume assumptions are acceptable without dedicated handling.
4. GTM: Sales has written refusal rules and cannot sell unsupported commitments.

If any of those remain “we could probably,” the answer should be no for Q3—not “yes with caveats.”

Planning implication

If this constrained version is genuinely committed for Q3, move the small-business-tier planning target to 65%. Keep the current 60% Q2 target unchanged until then.

Prep notes

Core framing

This is not a pricing-only decision. It is a product, operations, support, and sales-boundary decision. The question is whether we can offer a repeatable sub-50-seat product without letting every small account become a bespoke 200-seat implementation.

Recommended boundary

Sub-50 means 49 paid seats or fewer. Keep 50–75 in the starter framing; do not blur it into the 75–200 mid-segment definition.

Supportable in a Q3 launch

- Fixed seat cap and fixed entitlements
- Standard plan and billing flow
- Standard workspace and permission model
- Standard onboarding path with documentation and lightweight assistance
- Standard support channel and response expectations
- Standard import path where the product already supports it
- Clear upgrade path when the account outgrows the tier
- Sales can sell only what is in the published package

Custom-small-account pain / refuse by default

- Custom invoicing or contract terms
- Migration or data-cleaning services
- Bespoke permissions or workspace limits
- Dedicated onboarding or implementation help
- SSO/SCIM, audit-log, or other enterprise controls unless already productized for this tier
- Exceptions that let a sub-50 account buy individual pieces of the 75–200/enterprise operating model
- Manual entitlement overrides
- Sales promises that require Product, Engineering, or Support to make a one-off commitment

The sentence to use

“We can support a sub-50 offer in Q3 only if it is a bounded, repeatable product. If the launch requires exceptions in entitlements, onboarding, billing, migration, or support, then Q3 is not real for that version.”

Decision needed in the room

Q3 should be a yes only if all four owners can commit to the standard path:

1. Product: entitlement and feature fences are explicit.

Prep notes

Core framing

This is not a pricing-only decision. It is a product, operations, support, and sales-boundary decision. The question is whether we can offer a repeatable sub-50-seat product without letting every small account become a bespoke 200-seat implementation.

Recommended boundary

Sub-50 means 49 paid seats or fewer. Keep 50–75 in the starter framing; do not blur it into the 75–200 mid-segment definition.

Supportable in a Q3 launch

- Fixed seat cap and fixed entitlements
- Standard plan and billing flow
- Standard workspace and permission model
- Standard onboarding path with documentation and lightweight assistance
- Standard support channel and response expectations
- Standard import path where the product already supports it
- Clear upgrade path when the account outgrows the tier
- Sales can sell only what is in the published package

Custom-small-account pain / refuse by default

- Custom invoicing or contract terms
- Migration or data-cleaning services
- Bespoke permissions or workspace limits
- Dedicated onboarding or implementation help
- SSO/SCIM, audit-log, or other enterprise controls unless already productized for this tier
- Exceptions that let a sub-50 account buy individual pieces of the 75–200/enterprise operating model
- Manual entitlement overrides
- Sales promises that require Product, Engineering, or Support to make a one-off commitment

The sentence to use

“We can support a sub-50 offer in Q3 only if it is a bounded, repeatable product. If the launch requires exceptions in entitlements, onboarding, billing, migration, or support, then Q3 is not real for that version.”

Decision needed in the room

Q3 should be a yes only if all four owners can commit to the standard path:

1. Product: entitlement and feature fences are explicit.
2. Engineering/operations: onboarding, billing, workspace, permissions, and import paths work without manual intervention.
3. Support: the support model and volume assumptions are acceptable without dedicated handling.
4. GTM: Sales has written refusal rules and cannot sell unsupported commitments.

If any of those remain “we could probably,” the answer should be no for Q3—not “yes with caveats.”

Planning implication

If this constrained version is genuinely committed for Q3, move the small-business-tier planning target to 65%. Keep the current 60% Q2 target unchanged until then.

Use this order:

1. Helio Start: operating-model pre-discovery and gates
   - What we are deciding: whether the eligibility, refusal, entitlement, lifecycle, support, and capacity questions are understood well enough to continue.
   - Explicitly not a launch, pricing-page decision, or Q3 commitment.
   - Use the red/yellow/green gate framing; describe refusals as protecting customers from a failed self-serve setup.

   Transition:
   “That gives us the operating question: what would have to be true before this model is viable? Next, let’s make sure we can measure those conditions cleanly rather than debate them from mixed cuts.”

2. Measurement spine: baseline and instrumentation requirements
   - Baseline under activation definition v3.
   - Keep 75–200 paid seats as mid-segment v2 and show 50–75 separately.
   - Cover the event taxonomy and instrumentation for admin complexity, import/migration help, support handoff, entitlement state, and refusal reasons.
   - End with the minimum measurement work required before any test or launch decision.

   Transition:
   “This is the measurement spine for Helio Start. The next item is a different motion with a different population and decision rule, so I want to keep it separate rather than use it as supporting evidence for this work.”

3. Separate note: retained-mid expansion nudge
   - EXP-2023-05, in-product nudge, retained mid-segment v2 only.
   - Keep it as its own experiment readout; it is not evidence for Helio Start.
   - Treat the current result as directional usage-readiness evidence, not a broad expansion win or SMB signal.
   - No changes to copy, eligibility, or Helio Start framing based on this cut.

   Transition into close:
   “We’ll leave the expansion nudge with its own owner, population, and readout path. For Helio Start, the decision remains whether the operating and measurement gates are clear—not whether a separate retained-mid experiment is showing revenue potential.”

Opening line:

“I want to keep three motions distinct today: first, whether the Helio Start operating model is sufficiently understood; second, what measurement spine we need before making a decision; and third, a separate retained-mid experiment readout. The third should not be treated as evidence for the first.”

results.content:
I’d run the readout in this order:

1. Helio Start framing
   “Helio Start is still pre-discovery: we’re defining the operating model and its boundaries, not announcing a launch, pricing change, or Q3 commitment.”

2. Daniela’s gate
   Move immediately to the actual gate: eligibility versus product constraints, entitlement logic, feature fences, instrumentation/event taxonomy, and the handoffs across billing, permissions, imports, and support. The decision is whether the standard path is safe and measurable—not whether the pricing page can be ready.

3. Owen’s measurement spine
   Use Owen’s under-50 baseline, on activation v3, as the reference point for future cuts. Present it as a baseline and measurement setup, not evidence that Helio Start caused—or will cause—an activation change.

4. Ines’s lifecycle risk
   Describe the fork as conservative scope triage: reuse only the mechanically safe pieces, and hold anything dependent on eligibility, activation state, permissions, imports, admin structure, or support policy. No production fork, new trigger, or suppression until event mapping, duplicate-send behavior, and handoffs are agreed and QA’d.

5. Separate expansion-nudge learning
   Put this last or in a clearly separate section: the retained-mid expansion nudge is a behavior-based eligibility/readiness question within the 75–200-seat v2 cohort. It is directional learning about which retained-mid accounts may be ready for expansion—not a Helio Start result or proof that a sub-50 motion works.

Three lines I’d use verbatim:

“Helio Start is pre-discovery, not launch: the June output is a feasibility and scope decision, and any Q3 discussion remains conditional on clearing the gates.”

“Owen’s under-50 baseline gives us the measurement spine under activation v3; it is the comparison point for later evaluation, not causal evidence about Helio Start.”

“The expansion-nudge read is separate retained-mid behavior-based eligibility work: it may inform a readiness hypothesis, but it does not validate the Helio Start model.”

results.content: Assistant: Mentioned Q4 Lifecycle Systems contractor decision framework.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Riley Tanaka, message 003207
excerpts:
the team is trying to keep a full-time engagement busy.
- Concentrated execution can create more review load if outputs arrive faster than Owen, Ines, or other owners can validate them.

Recommended decision framework

1. Establish the workload baseline before comparing capacity

Create one inventory with:

- Work item and intended output
- Owner currently doing it
- Preparation versus judgment required
- Volume and recurrence
- Estimated preparation time
- Review and rework time
- Deadline or service expectation
- Dependencies on source data, engineering, Customer Success, or policy decisions
- Consequence if delayed
- Whether the work is suitable for delegation

The key measure is not contractor utilization. It is owner capacity returned: routine hours, review cycles, and context-switching removed from the existing team.

2. Separate steady-state demand from surge demand

Use the shape of the work to distinguish the cases:

- Low or manageable demand supports no contractor, provided the tradeoff is explicit.
- Recurring, distributed demand supports evaluating the half-time case.
- A defined, time-bound backlog supports evaluating the FTE case.
- If the demand pattern is unknown, none of the three cases has sufficient evidence yet.

3. Require an observable relief target

Before selecting an option, define what “relieved” means. For example:

- Riley no longer line-edits routine readouts after checks pass.
- Owen no longer performs manual inventory or evidence-packet assembly.
- Ines no longer absorbs routine documentation cleanup that is separate from lifecycle judgment.
- Review meetings spend less time reconstructing missing evidence.
- Audit preparation and operator enablement meet an agreed turnaround without displacing decision work.

The target should measure both work removed and work not displaced. A contractor who produces materials but adds equivalent review burden has not created meaningful relief.

4. Protect the owner lanes as a hard gate

The contractor may prepare, organize, reconcile against written rules, and identify missing evidence. The contractor may not become an owner, approver, or release path.

Existing lanes remain:

- Owen: measurement, denominators, evidence integrity, routine operating explanation, and the operating readout.
- Ines: lifecycle governance, messaging-state interpretation, and operator-facing guidance within her established lane.
- Daniela: engineering controls, source reliability, release, and rollback.
- Riley: disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, customer-correction or incident-stop decisions, higher-risk exceptions, and executive framing.
- Priya: the bounded business decision after the evidence and tradeoffs are separated.

These are not approval queues for every contractor output. The contractor’s work should be reviewable by the responsible owner through established checks, with escalation only for ambiguity, risk, or a decision that genuinely belongs to that owner.

5. Use option-specific gates rather than a general preference

No contractor passes only if:
- The measured workload fits current capacity.
- The team identifies no material displacement of higher-value work.
- The deferred-work consequences are accepted explicitly.

Half-time passes only if:
- The workload is recurring across the period.
- The work can be sustained at a half-time cadence.
- The expected owner-time relief is material.
- There is a clear mechanism for routine review without Riley becoming the reconciliation layer.

FTE passes only if:
- There is a documented backlog and deadline.
- The backlog is large enough to consume concentrated capacity.
- The work has defined completion criteria.
- The four-month exit and handoff are credible.

6. Keep evidence limits explicit

The decision should not rely on:

- General statements that the team is busy
- Contractor availability by itself
- A one-time spike without a documented backlog
- The number of tasks without effort or recurrence
- Claimed savings that ignore owner review and rework
- The assumption that preparation work establishes a need for new operating authority

The decision should remain a capacity decision, not a conclusion about product demand, staffing ratios, launch readiness, or organizational redesign.

Work that remains out of scope in all three cases

- A fifth shared-state consumer
- Helio Start paid acquisition
- Engineering release, production changes, or rollback control
- Replacement of Owen’s or Ines’s owner lanes
- New lifecycle authority or a new approval layer
- Contractor decisions on release, suppression, holds, customer contact, or customer correction
- Ownership assignments made by the contractor
- Reopening pricing, launch, beta-expansion, pipeline, or forecast decisions
- Treating prepared evidence as owner confirmation or release authorization

Decision posture

Do not choose among the three cases until the workload inventory establishes whether the demand is absent, recurring, or time-bound. The framework should select capacity based on workload shape and verified owner-time relief—not on the nominal size of the option or the desire to remove work from Riley informally.

input.body:
Q1 2024 LIFECYCLE CONTRACTOR ENGAGEMENT — RECONCILIATION WORKSHEET
As-of: 2028-01-01

Purpose
Reconcile the Q1 2024 lifecycle QA and operations contractor engagement using the earlier approval and the restored inbox messages. The approved envelope is a ceiling and is not evidence that the ceiling was fully spent.

1. Engagement control facts

Supported from the earlier approval and engagement record:

- Approved Q1 Growth envelope: $24,000.
- Engagement: lifecycle QA and operations contractor.
- Engagement dates: January 15–February 23, 2024, inclusive.
- Reporting owner / supervisor: Ines.
- Initial purchase-order / not-to-exceed cap: $23,180.
- Initial cap components: $20,400 professional services + $1,530 vendor administration fee + up to $1,250 tooling.
- Tooling condition: reimbursable only for tooling actually incurred, used, and approved; the allowance is not an automatic charge.
- Later approved bounded addition: up to 6 hours at $135/hour, or $810, for two operator-ready runbooks. The updated approved engagement ceiling was therefore $23,990 ($23,180 + $810), leaving $10 of the $24,000 envelope uncommitted if the entire updated ceiling had been used.

Permitted work categories:

- Active Customer.io campaign inventory.
- Experiment-setup hygiene.
- Suppression checks.
- Repeatable preflight work.
- Lifecycle QA and documentation/operations support under Ines.
- The separately approved, hard-capped runbook work: two bounded campaign runbooks with reproducible audience logic, suppression and duplicate-admin checks, copy-risk boundaries, release criteria, and rollback steps.

Boundary: preparation, documentation, and QA support only. The contractor did not receive approval authority, ownership authority, production-change authority, engineering release control, or authority to expand the strategy.

2. Observed charges from restored inbox subject lines

SUPPORTED

A. Invoice LC-101
- Subject: “Invoice LC-101 — Jan 15–Feb 2 lifecycle QA and preflight work — $8,400 — paid”
- Amount observed: $8,400.
- Period: January 15–February 2, 2024.
- Category: lifecycle QA and preflight work.
- Status: paid, per subject line.
- Scope/date assessment: supported as within the approved dates and permitted categories.

B. Invoice LC-102
- Subject: “Invoice LC-102 — Feb 3–16 lifecycle operations and suppression checks — $9,100 — paid”
- Amount observed: $9,100.
- Period: February 3–16, 2024.
- Category: lifecycle operations and suppression checks.
- Status: paid, per subject line.
- Scope/date assessment: supported as within the approved dates and permitted categories.

Supported observed subtotal
- LC-101: $8,400
- LC-102: $9,100
- Observed supported subtotal: $17,500

This is an observed subtotal, not a final engagement total.

3. Unresolved evidence and charges

UNRESOLVED

A. February 17–23 closeout billing
- Subject: “Q1 lifecycle contractor closeout — Feb 17–23 invoice and receipt still outstanding” from Ines.
- The subject establishes an outstanding invoice and receipt for February 17–23, but does not provide an amount, hours, rate, expense detail, tooling detail, or payment status.
- Do not estimate or book this period from the approved envelope alone.
- Required evidence: the invoice, itemized hours/work description, receipt support for any reimbursable tooling or expense, and confirmation that all work falls within the approved categories and engagement dates.

B. Approved runbook addition
- Up to $810 for six additional hours was approved for two bounded runbooks.
- No restored invoice subject line separately identifies a charge for that addition.
- Treat the approval as authorization, not as proof of performance or billing. Evidence remains unresolved unless the missing closeout invoice or supporting deliverable record ties hours and charges to the approved runbook scope.

C. Closeout completeness
- Final total spend, final hours, final expense/tooling amount, and final reconciliation status cannot be closed from the observed subjects alone because the February 17–23 invoice and receipt remain outstanding.
- The $17,500 supported subtotal should not be represented as full spend, and the $24,000 envelope should not be represented as spent.

4. Excluded items — do not charge to this engagement

EXCLUDED

A. Invoice HS-204
- Subject: “Invoice HS-204 — Helio Start paid acquisition setup — $2,600 — uncoded”
- Amount: $2,600.
- Status: uncoded, per subject line.
- Treatment: exclude from this engagement. Helio Start paid acquisition was explicitly outside the approved plan and received no allocation from this envelope. Route for separate approval/coding if appropriate; do not code it to the lifecycle contractor engagement.

B. Other prohibited or unauthorized activity
Do not charge any of the following to this engagement:

- Helio Start paid acquisition, paid-acquisition setup, launch, exposure, pricing, or pipeline work.
- Work outside January 15–February 23, 2024, unless separately approved under a new engagement or authorization.
- Campaign redesign or restructuring.
- New messaging, copy rewrites, new creative, or strategy expansion.
- New experiments or statistical analysis beyond the approved QA/preflight scope.
- Instrumentation changes or workflow migration.
- Engineering release work, production changes, release approval, rollback control, or reliability work.
- Assignment of campaign ownership, approval authority, release authority, or a new approval layer.
- Changes to unrelated live campaigns.
- Tooling or expenses not actually incurred, used, documented, and approved.
- Additional contractor hours beyond the approved scope and caps.

5. Reconciliation view

Approved envelope: $24,000
Initial PO / NTE cap: $23,180
Later approved runbook addition: $810
Updated approved engagement ceiling: $23,990
Observed supported charges: $17,500
Unresolved February 17–23 charges: amount not supplied
Excluded HS-204 charge: $2,600; not part of engagement spend

Known arithmetic against the observed supported subtotal:
- $24,000 envelope less $17,500 observed supported charges = $6,500 not yet supported as spent.
- $23,180 initial cap less $17,500 observed supported charges = $5,680 of initial cap not yet supported as spent.
- $23,990 updated ceiling less $17,500 observed supported charges = $6,490 of updated ceiling not yet supported as spent, before resolving the missing February 17–23 billing.

These are provisional balances pending the missing invoice and receipt. They are not authorization to spend, reallocate, or commit the balance.

6. Recommended accounting disposition

- Record LC-101 ($8,400) and LC-102 ($9,100) as supported observed engagement charges, subject to normal invoice-record retention.
- Hold the February 17–23 closeout item as unresolved pending the invoice, receipt, itemization, and scope/date check.
- Keep HS-204 ($2,600) excluded and uncoded to this engagement.
- Do not mark the $24,000 envelope fully spent or infer final utilization from the approved envelope.
- Do not reallocate any remaining balance to Helio Start paid acquisition or another workstream without separate approval and evidence.

Bottom line
The evidence currently supports $17,500 of lifecycle engagement charges. It does not establish the final total because February 17–23 billing evidence is outstanding. The $2,600 Helio Start paid-acquisition setup invoice is excluded and must not be charged to this engagement.

Q4 Development-Focus Review Aid
Owen and Ines
Review meeting: December 8, 2027

Purpose

Assess the completed October–December evidence against the approved development focuses. This aid records observable evidence only; it does not state the formal judgment before the meeting and does not expand either person’s authority.

1. Owen — Exception synthesis

Approved focus

Produce one exception synthesis per cycle that distinguishes:

- Source-certification delay
- Missing required input
- Cross-surface discrepancy
- Disputed semantics
- No-exception status

The synthesis should make evidence, coverage, affected lanes, limitations, ownership, and next action legible. Work should remain visibly incomplete when required inputs or semantics are unresolved, with escalation rather than unsupported closure.

Three-cycle evidence

- October: Identified a source-certification delay. The synthesis remained visibly incomplete until certified inputs arrived.
- November: Correctly reported no exception.
- December: Identified a source-certification delay. The synthesis remained visibly incomplete until certified inputs arrived.
- Across all three cycles: No missing field was concealed, and no semantic disagreement was represented as resolved.

Review prompts

- Did each synthesis distinguish the observed condition from interpretation?
- Was the work appropriately left open while certification was pending?
- Did the no-exception cycle avoid manufacturing an exception?
- Were the relevant limitations, ownership, and next actions clear?
- Did any case require escalation under the approved boundary?

Authority boundary

Owen’s role is evidence synthesis and recommendation within the routine reporting lane. He does not decide unresolved exceptions or disputed semantics and does not receive board-readiness, causal, revenue, forecast, customer-correction, incident-stop, engineering-release, rollback, or executive-language authority.

2. Ines — Lifecycle-risk explanation

Approved focus

Independently explain routine lifecycle-risk tradeoffs using existing governed states and lifecycle rules, distinguishing routine non-state-changing work from matters requiring escalation. The explanation should address audience risk, consequences of proceeding versus holding or suppressing, mitigation, and the responsible owner.

Three-cycle evidence

- Seven items were handled as routine, non-state-changing lifecycle-risk explanations.
- Two proposals involved state-changing work and were escalated to Riley before release.
- The evidence therefore includes both routine-risk reasoning and explicit handling of proposals outside routine authority.
- No state-changing proposal was released under routine authority.

Review prompts

- Did each explanation identify the triggering state and relevant audience or messaging risk?
- Were proceed, hold, suppress, or assisted-path consequences explained using existing meanings?
- Were mitigations and owner actions identified?
- Were state-changing or otherwise higher-risk proposals escalated before release?
- Did any explanation imply a new state meaning, release permission, or review-closure authority?

Authority boundary

Ines’s role is lifecycle-governance and routine lifecycle-risk explanation within existing controls. She may explain and recommend routine non-state-changing handling, but does not independently decide or release eligibility changes, state-meaning changes, customer corrections, incident-stop matters, disputed semantics, or engineering/release-control work. Existing review-closure, lifecycle-send, engineering-release, rollback, and higher-risk decision boundaries remain unchanged.

Meeting discipline

- Evaluate the evidence against the approved criteria, not against a presumed outcome.
- Separate quality of explanation from authority to decide or release.
- Record any remaining questions or evidence limits explicitly.
- Defer the formal judgment until the December 8 review is complete.

input.body:
2027 Lifecycle Systems development evidence — Ines and Owen

Year-end memo
Date: January 1, 2028
Decision/evidence basis: Q4 development-focus review completed December 8, 2027; Priya formally recorded both focuses as met.

Purpose
This memo records demonstrated behavior, the basis for completion, handling of exceptions and disputes, and the decision authority that did not transfer. Completion recognizes development within the existing owner and escalation lanes; it is not an authority expansion.

Ines

Demonstrated behaviors
- Across the October, November, and December cycles, Ines independently explained routine lifecycle-risk tradeoffs using existing governed states and lifecycle rules.
- She handled seven items as routine, non-state-changing lifecycle-risk explanations, identifying the relevant state and audience or messaging risk, the consequences of proceeding versus holding or suppressing, and the mitigation or responsible owner.
- In October, she classified an operator-note clarification as routine and non-state-changing because it changed no governed field or meaning, audience criterion, customer action, suppression, hold behavior, or release behavior.
- In November, she distinguished routine wording clarification from a state-changing proposal: treating held records as queued delivery would have changed governed behavior, so it required escalation before release.
- In December, she classified two operator-wording clarifications as routine and non-state-changing, while identifying the proposal to show the incomplete-setup reminder to non-admin users as state-changing because it expanded the audience. She escalated that proposal to Riley before release.
- No state-changing proposal was released under routine authority.

Basis for marking the development goal complete
The approved goal required one independent lifecycle-risk explanation per October, November, and December cycle, distinguishing routine non-state-changing work from escalation, explaining governed-state and audience risk, and not releasing higher-risk work under routine authority. The December 8 review found the complete three-cycle evidence: seven routine explanations and two state-changing proposals escalated before release. Priya recorded the focus as met. This demonstrates the intended reasoning and escalation behavior, not new release authority.

Exceptions and disputes
Ines preserved existing state meanings, lifecycle holds, suppression behavior, owner actions, and release boundaries. When a proposal affected audience, governed behavior, eligibility, state meaning, customer correction, incident-stop handling, disputed semantics, or another higher-risk area, she did not force a routine disposition or release; she held the matter and escalated it to Riley. Connector-specific wording work was treated separately from authority: the prior revision used paired cases to show unchanged triggers, owner action, governed meanings, holds, and suppression, with Daniela retaining connector-detection and release verification.

Decision authority not transferred by completion
Ines did not receive authority to decide or release eligibility changes, governed-state or state-meaning changes, customer corrections, incident stops, disputed semantics, higher-risk releases, review closure, lifecycle-send decisions outside the established routine lane, engineering release, or rollback. Daniela retains engineering release and rollback control; Riley retains disputed-semantics, customer-correction, incident-stop, and other higher-risk decision authority.

Owen

Demonstrated behaviors
- Across the October, November, and December cycles, Owen independently synthesized exceptions into clear, owner-ready explanations while keeping evidence boundaries visible.
- October: he identified a source-certification delay, kept the synthesis visibly incomplete while named-owner certification was absent, avoided stale substitution, and retained the delay in the closure summary after certification arrived.
- November: he correctly reported no exception; required sources had certified through-dates, required fields, and named-owner certification, with no source delay, missing input, cross-surface discrepancy, or disputed semantics.
- December: he again identified a source-certification delay and kept the synthesis visibly incomplete until certified inputs arrived.
- Across all three cycles, he did not conceal a missing field and did not represent a semantic disagreement as resolved.

Basis for marking the development goal complete
The approved goal required one exception synthesis per cycle distinguishing source-certification delay, missing required input, cross-surface discrepancy, disputed semantics, and no-exception status, while making evidence, coverage, affected lanes, limitations, ownership, and next action legible. Missing input or disputed semantics was to remain incomplete and come to Riley. The December 8 review found all three syntheses correct: two source-certification delays stayed visibly incomplete until certification, and one cycle correctly reported no exception. Priya recorded the focus as met. The result recognizes evidence synthesis and recommendation quality within the routine reporting lane.

Exceptions and disputes
Owen handled pending certification by leaving the work open rather than substituting stale data or manufacturing closure. He distinguished source delay from missing data, cross-surface discrepancy, disputed semantics, and no-exception status. Any missing required input or semantic dispute remains incomplete and is escalated rather than resolved by Owen. For any future semantic dispute, Owen must leave the review incomplete and escalate it to Riley Tanaka—the name established in Riley’s self-review and the standing escalation instruction.

Decision authority not transferred by completion
Owen did not receive authority to decide unresolved exceptions or disputed semantics, or to make board-readiness, causal, revenue, forecast, customer-correction, incident-stop, engineering-release, rollback, or executive-language claims or decisions. Completion does not transfer claim, readiness, narrative, or higher-risk decision authority. Riley retains disputed semantics and higher-risk decision authority; Daniela retains engineering release and rollback control.

Continuing boundaries
Both results are development outcomes within existing lanes, not a change to ownership or decision rights. Ines may explain and recommend routine non-state-changing handling but must escalate state-changing and higher-risk matters before release. Owen may synthesize routine reporting evidence and explain exceptions but must leave missing-input and semantic-dispute cases incomplete and escalate them to Riley Tanaka. Neither completion authorizes broader claims, release, rollback, customer correction, incident stop, executive language, revenue, forecast, causal, or board-readiness authority.

SAFE TO REUSE / ADAPT

1. Welcome and early onboarding structure
   Rationale: The welcome and day-3 paths have already gone through lifecycle QA. Reuse the sequencing and mechanical pattern, but adapt language for smaller teams rather than copying mid-segment positioning.

2. General activation-state messaging
   Rationale: The proven lesson is to match the message to the user’s state instead of sending every user the same thing on a calendar. The pattern is reusable; the actual eligibility fields and trigger implementation are not yet approved for sub-50.

3. Low-risk educational copy
   Examples: first-value guidance, basic setup prompts, explaining how teams use the product without implying entitlement to particular features.
   Rationale: This does not require a finalized support model or a promise that the account qualifies for a specific product path.

4. Email-template and compliance mechanics
   Examples: token fallbacks, locale handling, rendering checks, footer/unsubscribe behavior, and old Customer.io branch cleanup.
   Rationale: These are established QA requirements and are independent of the tier decision. They should still be re-tested on every adapted variant.

5. The “diagnose before changing the journey” workflow
   Rationale: Keep the existing discipline of checking activation state, event mapping, duplicate sends, and cohort definitions before turning a fork into production behavior. This avoids another pile of untracked copy edits.

NEEDS AN ELIGIBILITY OR SUPPORT DECISION

1. The day-7 “See how teams use Helio” touch
   Rationale: The copy may be adaptable, but the existing calendar-day-7, state-blind rule is not a safe basis for the new tier. Decide whether it applies to activated users, unactivated users, both, or neither.

2. Activation-triggered versus calendar-triggered forks
   Rationale: The activation-triggered pattern worked in the earlier mid-segment work, but that does not automatically establish eligibility or event behavior for sub-50. Confirm the activation definition, late-activation behavior, suppression rule, and duplicate-send protection.

3. The canonical seat-band rule
   Rationale: The current work is described as sub-50, while the small-business planning scope has been framed as 20–75 seats. Decide whether eligibility is based on current paid seats, signup seats, projected seats, or another account-level field.

4. Support CTAs and human-help language
   Examples: “talk to an expert,” migration assistance, onboarding help, workspace setup, or priority response.
   Rationale: These are operational commitments, not just copy. Support needs to specify what is included, what is self-serve, and what happens when an account falls outside the supported path.

5. Sales-assist and exception routing
   Rationale: Decide whether a small account can request sales help, when it is routed to Sales or Support, and who can approve exceptions. Otherwise lifecycle copy may create commitments the operating model cannot fulfill.

6. Feature-specific branches
   Examples: SSO, audit logs, permissions, workspace limits, custom invoicing, import/migration, or other enterprise-oriented capabilities.
   Rationale: Each branch depends on entitlement and support policy. These should not be treated as harmless personalization until Product, Billing, Engineering, and Support agree on the fence.

7. “Upgrade,” “expand,” or “contact us for more” prompts
   Rationale: These imply a commercial or sales path. They need a clear eligibility rule and an owner for the resulting handoff, especially given the concern about Sales selling unsupported commitments.

DEFINITELY NOT SAFE YET

1. Copy that promises unsupported features or services
   Examples: guaranteed migration help, custom invoicing, human onboarding, SSO, audit logs, or priority support.
   Rationale: The small-business work explicitly requires deciding what we refuse to support. Until that matrix exists, these promises should be parked.

2. Reusing the mid-segment eligibility logic unchanged
   Rationale: The existing onboarding-trigger work was scoped to the old 50–200-seat mid-segment and later operationalized around 75–200 paid seats. It is evidence for a lifecycle pattern, not evidence that the same fork or thresholds apply to sub-50 accounts.

3. A blanket “all sub-50 accounts get this journey” rule
   Rationale: It would collapse potentially different cases—trial versus paid, current versus invited seats, activated versus unactivated, and supported versus unsupported configurations—before eligibility is defined.

4. The current state-blind calendar-day-7 journey as the default
   Rationale: It sends activated and cold users the same message on the same clock. That was already identified as a lifecycle weakness and should not become the starting point for the new tier.

5. Production flag or trigger changes
   Rationale: Do not create a sub-50 fork, widen an existing flag, or suppress existing touches until the eligibility rule, event mapping, duplicate-send behavior, and support handoff are agreed and QA’d.

6. Performance claims or target language
   Examples: implying that the fork will raise activation, citing the mid-segment retention lift, or using the conditional 65% small-business activation target as if it were already current.
   Rationale: The 65% target was conditional on the tier actually shipping in Q3. It should not appear as established evidence in lifecycle copy.

7. Any “refusal” copy shown directly to customers
   Rationale: The team needs explicit exclusion rules, but internal refusal boundaries are not automatically customer-ready wording. First decide the policy, then write customer-safe explanations.

Recommended Monday decision order:

1. Lock the canonical eligibility band and seat-count definition.
2. Define supported versus unsupported features and services.
3. Decide the Sales/Support handoff and exception rules.
4. Define activation-state and trigger behavior.
5. Only then adapt the copy and build the fork.
6. Keep the existing email QA checklist and measurement separation intact.

input.title: Historical Cohort-Cut Template — Concurrent Experiment Lanes
input.body:
STATUS / SCOPE
Historical archive template only. This documents the operating pattern used while two experiments were live concurrently; it does not assign current work, indicate current experiment status, authorize a rollout, or create a standing obligation.

WEEKLY OPERATING PATTERN
- Cadence: Every Monday.
- Historical weekly owner: Owen.
- Method: Run both lanes in parallel using the same format, definitions, and reporting order. Keep the lanes analytically separate; do not combine their denominators, metrics, or conclusions.

HISTORICAL EXPERIMENT LANES
1. Pricing-page lane
   - Historical read: pricing-page weekly cohort cut.
   - Record the experiment identifier, exposure window, cohort definition, metric of record, arms, and exclusions.
2. Onboarding-trigger lane
   - Historical read: onboarding weekly cohort cut.
   - Record the experiment identifier, exposure window, cohort definition, metric of record, arms, and exclusions.

REQUIRED PACKAGE FOR EACH LANE
1. Summary first — one-page scan-first readout containing:
   - Cohort and exposure window; experiment identifier and scope.
   - Denominator (n) by arm and any exclusions, censoring, or maturity limits.
   - Primary metric and result by arm; absolute effect size and, where supported, p-value or confidence interval.
   - Pre-declared segment cuts only; include composition, sample-ratio, and signup-source checks when relevant.
   - Data-quality notes, cohort-over-cohort drift/stability, and practical interpretation.
   - Conclusion and open caveats; do not treat first significance as sufficient for a ship decision—retain any stabilization-cohort boundary.
2. Raw data underneath — attach the reproducible underlying cohort-level export/query output, preserving raw fields and timestamps. Include the query or extract version, filters, metric definitions, arm labels, denominators, and a data dictionary/notes sufficient to reproduce the summary.

PACKAGING RULE
For every Monday delivery, place the one-page summary above its matching raw-data attachment for each lane. Label lane, cohort window, and generation date clearly. Preserve the two lane packages separately in the archive; never substitute a combined total for the lane-level reads.

ARCHIVE NOTE
Use this template only to describe or reconstruct the historical concurrent-read pattern. Any future analysis or assignment requires a separate, current decision and owner designation.

results.content:
Here’s a tightened, ready-to-paste version.

Opener

Helio Start is an internal exploration of how to make self-serve workable for smaller teams while protecting customers from being placed in a setup that the product, integrations, or support model cannot reliably support.

This pre-read proposes working eligibility boundaries, customer-protective non-support rules, measurement requirements, and operational dependencies for engineering scoping. It is not a final launch policy, public pricing decision, or commitment to a Q3 launch.

The baseline is descriptive, not causal: it shows current patterns in the data but does not establish why they occur. In particular, first-week integration is an observed signal, not evidence that integration alone creates activation or that Helio Start would improve activation. Any causal interpretation will require stable definitions, complete instrumentation, and an appropriate comparison design.

Risk labels

Green — Supported for current self-serve path
The product, integration, billing, and support experience appears able to serve this case reliably. Continue validation through the standard measurement and readiness checks.

Yellow — Requires validation before customer exposure
A dependency or uncertainty could make setup, product use, billing, or support unreliable. Resolve the dependency and validate the customer experience before making a customer-facing promise.

Red — Not yet supported for reliable self-serve setup
The current operating model cannot reliably support this case without a material risk of failed setup or poor customer experience. Keep it outside the self-serve path until the relevant product, engineering, lifecycle, or support capability is in place.

Language replacements

- “Bad fit” → “Not yet supported for a reliable self-serve setup”
- “Cheap plan” → “Helio Start” or “smaller-team self-serve path”
- “Refused account” → “Case we do not currently support through self-serve”
- “Ineligible customer” → “Use case outside the current supported boundary”

A short label key for the table could be:

Green: Supported
Yellow: Validate before exposure
Red: Protect customer from failed self-serve setup

results.content:
Helio Start Q4 closeout — January readiness gate

Decision frame

Helio Start remains a capped, invite-only controlled beta for selected sub-50-seat accounts. The January discussion is a readiness gate for whether the operating model is sufficiently bounded and measurable to continue under the current constraints or support a separately considered access decision.

This is not setup for a Q1 launch. It does not pre-commit to GA, pricing-page exposure, paid acquisition, broader beta access, pipeline treatment, forecast credit, or revenue recognition.

What the evidence says

1. Supported path is working for a narrow cohort

- November: 24 manually reviewed invitations; 19 accepted.
- 13 accepted invitees confirmed admin ownership.
- 6 were routed to Customer Success before setup:
  - 3 were not the workspace owner.
  - 1 involved a shared-agency OAuth domain.
  - 1 had IT-controlled SSO ownership.
  - 1 had delegated setup to a contractor.
- 9 new workspaces were created; 8 reached first integration.
- Earlier Q4 evidence also showed 20 live beta accounts and 18 de-duplicated first-integration attempts.

2. Support routing is becoming measurable

- Support load is lower than in August and September, particularly around billing and import handoffs.
- The earlier support mix showed:
  - 12 permissions/admin-ownership questions.
  - 7 billing-expectation questions.
  - 4 import/migration-expectation questions.
  - 11 ordinary API-key/setup questions handled docs-first.
- The six November pre-setup CS routes did not require manual billing or import support.

3. Admin proof is useful, but not solved

- Moving admin-ownership proof earlier is routing uncertainty before setup rather than forcing it through the beta path.
- The shared-agency case and other ownership edge cases show that admin proof remains the primary watch item.
- The evidence is directional and operational. It does not establish that admin attestation causes higher activation or lower support load.

4. Instrumentation is sufficient only if its semantics remain intact

- Entitlement is captured at workspace creation.
- Support-state changes are recorded through the defined handoff and billing events.
- Legacy nulls must be annotated or routed through the documented operations-review path.
- Entitlement must not be inferred from plan name.
- Helio Start activation and support reporting remain separate from retained-mid and Expansion Assist.

What the evidence does not show

- Broad self-serve readiness.
- Generalization beyond the selected, capped cohort.
- A solved admin experience.
- Causal impact from admin attestation.
- Demand, willingness to pay, pipeline lift, revenue impact, or pricing readiness.
- Readiness for a launch, GA, pricing-page exposure, or broader access.

Operating guardrails that remain in force

Eligibility and routing

- Admit only selected accounts under 50 seats with complete eligibility information, a simple deployment path, and clean administrator ownership.
- Seat count alone is not eligibility.
- Unclear ownership, permissions complexity, inherited integrations, shared-admin cases, and other unresolved ownership questions route to assisted handling.
- Do not force edge cases through the self-serve beta.

Unsupported paths

The beta does not support:

- Manual billing exceptions.
- Migration or import assistance.
- General setup assistance beyond ordinary docs-first integration/API-key support.
- Lifecycle messaging that promises support, entitlement changes, billing resolution, import help, or ownership resolution.
- State-changing lifecycle actions where entitlement or support ownership is unresolved.
- Customer.io or equivalent proxy automation for billing mismatch, import-stuck, or support-handoff branches.

Lifecycle boundary

- Continue only bounded, non-state-changing education, such as setup-checklist and first-integration preparation.
- Keep the unsupported lifecycle list explicit in every relevant path.
- Lifecycle copy cannot paper over an eligibility, admin-ownership, entitlement, billing, import, or support-routing blocker.

Measurement boundary

- Primary support metric: support questions per invite acceptance.
- Secondary experience metric: support questions per active beta account.
- Keep “routed to CS before setup” visible beside post-workspace support load; it is part of the admin-quality gate, not noise to remove.
- Keep Helio Start activation separate from retained-mid and Expansion Assist.
- Review activation, first integration, support-load mix, and handoff quality together.

January readiness questions

The January gate should answer:

1. Admin proof
   - What constitutes clean admin-ownership proof?
   - Which recurring cases remain assisted by definition?
   - Are we reducing avoidable handoffs, or only moving the check earlier?

2. Support load
   - Are support-load comparisons using both invite-acceptance and active-account denominators?
   - Are pre-setup CS routes and post-workspace questions visible together?
   - Is the lower billing/import load durable, and what remains concentrated in admin ownership?

3. Activation and first integration
   - What first-integration level is sufficient for continued learning?
   - Does activation remain acceptable once support-load mix and handoff quality are included?
   - Are we avoiding an “activation win” claim from the admin-proof change alone?

4. Entitlement instrumentation
   - Is the canonical entitlement state complete at workspace creation and through support/billing transitions?
   - Are legacy unknowns clearly marked rather than inferred?
   - Is the event taxonomy reliable enough to support any later access decision?

5. Unsupported lifecycle list
   - Are the refusal and assisted-path rules being applied consistently?
   - Are lifecycle messages staying education-only?
   - Which unsupported cases remain hard stops regardless of improved support signals?

Recommended decision

Keep Helio Start capped and non-public through the January readiness review. Use the review to determine whether the operating evidence is durable enough to continue the bounded beta under the existing rules—not whether the program is prepared for a Q1 launch.

Suggested executive wording

“Helio Start has produced useful evidence from a narrow, controlled cohort: selected accounts are reaching first integration, pre-setup admin uncertainty is being routed earlier, and billing/import handoffs are lower. The evidence does not establish broad self-serve readiness, a solved admin experience, or launch readiness. January is a readiness gate on support load, admin proof, entitlement instrumentation, and the unsupported lifecycle boundary. It is not a Q1 launch plan or launch claim.”

Owner readout

- Daniela: entitlement and support-state instrumentation integrity.
- Owen: separate activation/support dashboard and denominator discipline.
- Ines: conservative lifecycle fork and explicit unsupported list.
- Customer Success: assisted routing and handoff-quality evidence.
- Riley: decision boundary, guardrails, and executive framing.

input.title: 2028 Self-Serve Operating Model Annual Review — Kickoff Agenda
input.body:
2028 Self-Serve Operating Model Annual Review — Kickoff Agenda
Date: January 1, 2028
Purpose: Review how the existing self-serve operating model performed, where evidence is incomplete, and which operating decisions or guardrails need attention in 2028. This is an operating review, not an org change or reporting-line announcement.

1. Operating frame and decision boundaries — Riley (10 min)
- Reconfirm the current self-serve boundary: eligibility and product constraints stay distinct; unsupported or unresolved cases route to assisted handling.
- Review high-stakes cuts, cross-surface tradeoffs, decision rules, and executive-language claims.
- Identify decisions, exceptions, and gates for 2028; do not reopen routine owner responsibilities.

2. Measurement integrity and exception reporting — Owen (10 min)
- Review definitions, denominators, units of analysis, source ownership, and exception handling.
- Keep Helio Start/self-serve reporting separate from retained mid-segment and Expansion Assist.
- Surface only disputed semantics, material exceptions, and evidence gaps; routine reporting remains with its owner.

3. Lifecycle governance and message-state controls — Ines (8 min)
- Review lifecycle paths, message-state controls, suppression/hold rules, and unsupported-state handling.
- Confirm that education can continue only where eligibility, entitlement, ownership, and support boundaries are clear.

4. Event, entitlement, and support-state reliability — Daniela’s team (8 min)
- Review event taxonomy, canonical entitlement state, handoffs, and source/release reliability.
- Mark unresolved instrumentation or state-contract items as gates; do not infer missing states from plan names or downstream outcomes.

5. Balanced operating read — group (10 min)
Review the measures together, without collapsing them into one score:
- Activation and first integration: outcome and experience signals for the supported self-serve path.
- Support load: coequal operating measure beside activation, including ordinary admitted support and its mix.
- Pre-admission eligibility/ownership contacts and assisted-before-setup routing: visible separately from admitted support load and activation denominators.
- Handoff quality, unsupported-case incidence, entitlement/state integrity, and lifecycle safety: guardrails that qualify the read.
- Evidence limits: distinguish descriptive patterns from causal, revenue, forecast, or broad-readiness claims.

6. Decisions and next review cycle — Riley (4 min)
- Record: decided, owner-ready, blocked/gated, and requires executive decision.
- Assign the smallest next evidence or operating action, owner, source, and review date.
- Preserve the current accountability lanes; this kickoff does not create a new team or reporting line.

document.body:
2028 Self-Serve Operating Model Annual Review — Kickoff Agenda
Date: January 1, 2028
Purpose: Review how the existing self-serve operating model performed, where evidence is incomplete, and which operating decisions or guardrails need attention in 2028. This is an operating review, not an org change or reporting-line announcement.

1. Operating frame and decision boundaries — Riley (10 min)
- Reconfirm the current self-serve boundary: eligibility and product constraints stay distinct; unsupported or unresolved cases route to assisted handling.
- Review high-stakes cuts, cross-surface tradeoffs, decision rules, and executive-language claims.
- Identify decisions, exceptions, and gates for 2028; do not reopen routine owner responsibilities.

2. Measurement integrity and exception reporting — Owen (10 min)
- Review definitions, denominators, units of analysis, source ownership, and exception handling.
- Keep Helio Start/self-serve reporting separate from retained mid-segment and Expansion Assist.
- Surface only disputed semantics, material exceptions, and evidence gaps; routine reporting remains with its owner.

3. Lifecycle governance and message-state controls — Ines (8 min)
- Review lifecycle paths, message-state controls, suppression/hold rules, and unsupported-state handling.
- Confirm that education can continue only where eligibility, entitlement, ownership, and support boundaries are clear.

4. Event, entitlement, and support-state reliability — Daniela’s team (8 min)
- Review event taxonomy, canonical entitlement state, handoffs, and source/release reliability.
- Mark unresolved instrumentation or state-contract items as gates; do not infer missing states from plan names or downstream outcomes.

5. Balanced operating read — group (10 min)
Review the measures together, without collapsing them into one score:
- Activation and first integration: outcome and experience signals for the supported self-serve path.
- Support load: coequal operating measure beside activation, including ordinary admitted support and its mix.
- Pre-admission eligibility/ownership contacts and assisted-before-setup routing: visible separately from admitted support load and activation denominators.
- Handoff quality, unsupported-case incidence, entitlement/state integrity, and lifecycle safety: guardrails that qualify the read.
- Evidence limits: distinguish descriptive patterns from causal, revenue, forecast, or broad-readiness claims.

6. Decisions and next review cycle — Riley (4 min)
- Record: decided, owner-ready, blocked/gated, and requires executive decision.
- Assign the smallest next evidence or operating action, owner, source, and review date.
- Preserve the current accountability lanes; this kickoff does not create a new team or reporting line.

Desired output: a short decision log and 2028 review cadence, with every material claim naming its source, accountable owner, unit of analysis, denominator, and decision boundary.

results.content:
Helio Start Q3 closeout — meeting frame

Opening frame

“We are closing Q3 on what the current operating model can support, what it cannot support, and whether we agree to keep Q4 as a controlled learning beta. This is not a launch or pricing decision, and the admin path is not solved.”

1. What Helio Start has support for

- A narrow, non-public controlled beta for selected sub-50-seat accounts.
- Entry through the invite path, not the public pricing page.
- Candidates with complete eligibility information, simple deployment, and a clear named administrator.
- Earlier admin-ownership proof as a customer-protective gate. It prevents avoidable support handoffs; it does not mean the underlying admin experience is solved.
- Ordinary integration and API-key/setup questions handled through docs-first support.
- Explicit routing for entitlement, support, billing, and lifecycle state.
- Separate measurement of sub-50 activation, support load, and retained-mid performance.
- Conservative lifecycle communication that does not create a state-changing or support promise beyond the beta boundary.

2. What Helio Start does not support

- It does not support a general self-serve path when admin ownership or permissions are unclear.
- It does not support manual billing exceptions.
- It does not support migration or import assistance inside the beta path.
- It does not support treating seat count alone as eligibility.
- It does not support assuming the admin path is fixed because proof is now collected earlier.
- It does not support public pricing-page exposure, paid acquisition, or broad beta widening.
- It does not support launch language, a Q4 revenue claim, forecast credit, or retrospective Q3 revenue credit.
- It does not support folding Helio Start into the retained-mid or Expansion Assist read.
- Unresolved cases should be held out of the self-serve beta and routed to the appropriate assisted path—not forced through as edge cases.

3. Q4 controlled-beta operating shape to ask Tomás to accept

Ask Tomás to accept this:

“Keep Helio Start capped and non-public through Q4 as a controlled operating-model beta. Admit only accounts that meet the documented deployment, eligibility, and admin-proof requirements. Treat unclear admin ownership, permissions complexity, billing exceptions, and migration/import needs as assisted paths. Review activation together with support-load mix and handoff quality, with no pricing-page exposure, paid acquisition, launch framing, or revenue/forecast credit. Revisit widening only after the admin-ownership and support evidence is durable enough to show that we are reducing avoidable handoffs—not merely moving the check earlier.”

Decision to leave the room with

- Tomás accepts “capped controlled beta” as the Q4 posture.
- The admin-proof check is accepted as a guardrail, not represented as a solved admin experience.
- Daniela, Owen, Ines, and Support retain explicit operating owners for entitlement/state, measurement, lifecycle, and handoffs.
- Any future widening requires a separate evidence-based gate; it is not implied by Q4 planning.

input.title: Expansion Assist second cohort — eligibility integrity decision
input.body:
Decision date: 2028-01-01

Decision
The second bounded Expansion Assist cohort retained the locked evidence-complete roster of 15 candidates. The operational capacity allowance was an upper bound—18 accounts, with no more than three exposures per week—not a target or a reason to admit additional accounts. Capacity described how much approved work could be handled; it did not change the evidence required for eligibility.

Eligibility was not relaxed to use the remaining three-account headroom. Accounts lacking the required evidence, including the applicable integration, currently active qualifying-admin, and recent product-visible usage-ceiling checks, or subject to Customer Success adoption or renewal suppression, were not substituted into the cohort. No marginal-account replacement, acceleration, or eligibility rewrite was authorized.

Interpretation
The unused headroom is deliberate unallocated capacity, preserving the cohort’s evidence and governance boundary.
