arguments.body:
Q1 2027 Lifecycle Systems operating priorities
Staff-review draft for December 18

Purpose and operating boundary
Q1 priorities are to run the approved January 5, 2027 operating model, keep the existing four-consumer shared-state contract reliable, make evidence closure repeatable, and keep every growth or lifecycle decision evidence-gated. This is an operating-priorities draft, not a new authority decision, production expansion, launch plan, or budget approval.

January 5 model and the current-through-January-4 distinction
- Through January 4, 2027, the current operating model and current owner attendance/cadence remain in force; nothing takes effect early.
- Beginning January 5, the approved model delegates routine monthly preparation and source-closure attendance while preserving a concrete monthly hands-on audit for Riley to test the evidence system directly.
- The delegated model does not change field meanings, consumer scope, lifecycle-send limits, engineering release or rollback control, customer-correction or incident-stop authority, or the standards for causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, and final-claim decisions.

Existing production consumers and field meanings
The scope remains exactly four production consumers:
1. Helio Start reporting — uses the governed state for reporting; it does not turn reporting evidence into a paid-acquisition, pipeline, or forecast conclusion.
2. Expansion Assist selection — uses the same governed state plus its own selection and Customer Success conditions; it remains a narrow, descriptive retained-mid lane, outside causal lift, revenue commitments, pipeline, and forecast credit.
3. Lifecycle preflight — uses the governed state for prompt/message eligibility, suppression, hold, and routing decisions; it does not create lifecycle-send release authority.
4. CS auto-nudge — remains within the existing routine messaging-state review and guidance lane; it is not a blanket closure authority across the other consumers and does not widen the four-consumer scope.

Across the consumers, the five governed fields remain distinct and retain their current meanings: external-system authority, connector authentication, entitlement, qualifying-human-admin status, and active Customer Success adoption or renewal work. Each field has its own source owner, as-of time, and freshness limit. Missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state remains visible as a field-specific fail-closed hold. No consumer may reuse a prior eligible value, silently change a meaning, or override a hold.

First January cycle and incomplete handling
- Start the first January cycle under the January 5 model, using the existing cadence: sanitized preparation, lifecycle-governance/message-state review, denominator/definition/source-completeness review, and routing of governed issues to the appropriate escalation lane.
- Establish the cycle baseline by lane and consumer: source and as-of coverage, denominator, evaluated records, visible holds/exceptions, owner and disposition, and any disagreement between source, operational treatment, and reported language.
- Mark an item incomplete when a required source, denominator, cohort/coverage date, owner review, certification, or decision input is missing; when an exception remains unresolved; or when the evidence does not support the proposed interpretation.
- Incomplete is an explicit status, not a gap to fill by inference. Do not mark an item complete, board-ready, released, or approved because a deadline passed or a neighboring lane is complete. Keep the item open/held/not board-ready, record the missing input and owner, and carry it into the next cycle or escalate it under the standing triggers.

Quarterly post-closure one-lane recheck
After quarterly closure, run one bounded recheck of one selected evidence lane against source, operational treatment, and reported language. Rotate the lane over time while preserving coverage of all four lanes. The recheck tests the closed record; it does not reopen the quarter, change a field meaning, create a new consumer, grant closure authority, or convert a discrepancy into a claim. Any discrepancy routes to the established owner and escalation lane.

Separate evidence lanes
Keep these four lanes separate in every Q1 review and staff/board preparation:
- Helio Start: bounded operating evidence; no automatic acquisition, pipeline, revenue, or forecast inference.
- Expansion Assist: descriptive retained-mid behavior and handoff evidence; no causal or forecast inference.
- Pricing-page path quality: test, attribution, continuity, and release-path evidence; not a substitute for Helio Start cohort evidence.
- System controls: CS auto-nudge and lifecycle-governance/control reliability; report control performance, not growth or revenue impact.
Never blend the lanes into one growth row or transfer readiness from one lane to another.

Established decision-owner boundaries
- Owen: reporting semantics, definitions, denominators, routine operating explanation, source-completeness review, and exception reporting. Owen may close source completeness within that bounded lane; he does not decide disputed semantics, causal/revenue/forecast interpretation, board readiness, or final executive claims.
- Ines: lifecycle governance, message-state consumption, routine messaging-state review, and related operator guidance. Her routine lane does not close Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, or lifecycle preflight; it does not change lifecycle-send release limits.
- Daniela and Engineering: transport, source reliability, instrumentation, engineering release, and rollback controls. Daniela retains engineering release/rollback authority; reliability work does not silently alter semantics or authorize customer actions.
- Riley: disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, high-stakes cuts, customer corrections, incident stops, state-changing, ambiguous or exception-heavy matters, and executive language/claims, including causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, and final-claim decisions. Riley's monthly hands-on audit is a test of the system, not a return to routine row-by-row preparation.
- Priya: sponsor for organizational and resource constraints. Marcus retains forecast ownership, and Tomás retains final board narrative authority.

Separate future paid Helio Start question
Whether to prepare or consider a future paid Helio Start question remains separate from these Q1 operating priorities. Nothing here approves paid traffic, a paid batch, acquisition activity, budget, pipeline treatment, forecast credit, or launch language. Any future paid proposal requires its own decision and separate budget approval, while existing eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, instrumentation, and support-routing safeguards remain unchanged.

Owner-lane input update — December 15, 2026

For the first January cycle, the operating test must explicitly cover:
- on-time snapshot preparation;
- named-owner certification; and
- a visibly incomplete state whenever any required field or certification is absent.

The cycle must remain open until it closes. Do not call it successful before closure, and do not infer completeness or success from preparation alone.

Ines’s owner certification is an input to source closure. It is not a request for Riley’s routine approval. The certification remains within Ines’s lifecycle-governance owner lane and contributes to the source-closure record under the existing boundaries.

Unchanged boundaries: the January 5, 2027 effective date remains in force; Riley continues current routine preparation and source-closure attendance through January 4; Daniela retains release and rollback ownership; and all existing claims, authority, consumer-scope, evidence, and non-authorization boundaries remain unchanged. Priya’s December 18 staff review remains pending.

Status update — December 18, 2026

Priya’s December 18 staff review is complete. Priya accepted this document for implementation use without changing the approved operating model. The approved model remains effective January 5, 2027; nothing changes early.

Through January 4, Riley remains in routine monthly preparation and source-closure reviews. Beginning January 5, Owen owns the stated preparation cadence and the explicit-complete-or-incomplete closure cadence: the monthly sanitized campaign snapshot remains due on the second business day; Ines’s lifecycle-governance and owner-state certification and Daniela’s source-reliability and release certification remain due by the fourth business day; and by the fifth business day Owen closes the routine four-lane source review or explicitly leaves it incomplete and sends one closure-and-exception summary.

Ines’s certification is an owner input, not a request for Riley’s routine approval. Daniela retains release and rollback ownership. Riley’s quarterly one-lane recheck remains in place after Owen closes the packet and does not reopen source closure, approve Ines’s certification, or exercise Daniela’s release or rollback controls. The established causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, and executive-language lanes remain unchanged, as do the existing escalation triggers and final-claim boundaries.

The future paid Helio Start question remains separate and is not traffic or budget authorization.

January 15, 2027 final decision — source-readiness check

Owen will run a monthly source-readiness check at noon Central on the business day before each sanitized campaign snapshot is due. Every required source must show a named owner, its exact certified-through date, and a certification ETA. If an ETA falls after the snapshot deadline, Owen marks that cycle at risk. If certification is still absent on the due date, Owen opens the snapshot visibly incomplete rather than using stale data.

This decision does not change the second-business-day deadline, the owner-certification requirement, freshness limits, source meanings, existing authority, or fail-closed handling.

Label revision — source-readiness and snapshot-certification wording

Replace the three operational labels with:

1. Source readiness: On track
   All required sources have named owners, exact owner-certified through-dates, and ETAs no later than the snapshot deadline; this is a readiness signal, not certification or closure.

2. Source readiness: At risk
   At least one required source has an ETA after the snapshot deadline; the packet remains open, with no stale or provisional substitute.

3. Snapshot certification: Blocked — certification missing

Escalation remains unchanged: Owen should notify the named source owner and route the exception through the existing path; he may not waive a missing source or certification, change freshness rules, or override fail-closed handling. These labels describe source readiness and snapshot certification only, not customer-account or messaging state. The January 15 deadline, owner-certification requirement, freshness limits, source meanings, existing authority, and fail-closed handling remain unchanged.

## February operating-model check
January 29 was preparation only. Owen’s February 1 readiness check showed on-time certification ETAs but did not itself certify any source. All certified sources arrived before the February 2 deadline, and Owen prepared the 141-campaign snapshot on February 2. Ines completed lifecycle-governance and owner-state certification and Daniela completed source-reliability and release certification by February 4. Owen closed the routine four-lane review on February 5 with no remaining exception. I did not attend the routine close. My separate January 29 one-lane quarterly audit did not reopen source closure or create a second approval queue.

Priya concluded that the February monthly source cycle operated as designed: the readiness check exposed certification timing without certifying inputs; named owners completed their certifications; Owen closed the routine packet; Riley did not attend routine closure; and the separate one-lane quarterly audit did not create a second approval queue. No change was made to the January 5 operating model, owner boundaries, deadlines, or quarterly audit cadence. 2027 Lifecycle Systems leadership model — December 4 approved decision record

Decision date: December 4, 2026
Approver: Priya
Effective date: January 5, 2027

Decision

Priya approved the Lifecycle Systems operating model in the December 4 decision meeting. The model becomes effective January 5, 2027. No attendance or authority change takes effect before January 5.

Transition boundary: through January 4, Riley continues the current routine preparation and source-closure attendance. Nothing changes early.

Delegated monthly operating cadence

1. Owen — by the second business day
   Deliver the monthly sanitized campaign snapshot.

2. Ines — by the fourth business day
   Complete lifecycle-governance and owner-state certification.

3. Daniela — by the fourth business day
   Complete source-reliability and release certification.

4. Owen — by the fifth business day
   Close the routine four-lane source review, or explicitly leave it incomplete, and send one closure-and-exception summary.

Riley’s operating role beginning January 5

Beginning January 5, Riley stops attending routine monthly preparation and closure reviews. Riley enters the operating process when any of the following requires attention:

- missing required fields;
- disputed semantics;
- cross-surface discrepancies;
- customer corrections or incident stops; or
- causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, or executive-language decisions.

Quarterly independent recheck

Once per quarter, after Owen closes the packet, Riley selects one lane and independently rechecks:

- its denominator or coverage dates;
- outcome window;
- exclusions;
- reliability evidence; and
- revenue and forecast treatment.

The quarterly recheck is an independent evidence check. It does not reopen source closure, approve Ines’s certification, or exercise Daniela’s release or rollback controls.

Authority and non-authority boundaries

- Owen remains responsible for the routine sanitized campaign snapshot, the routine four-lane source review, closure or explicit incomplete status, and the closure-and-exception summary.
- Ines remains responsible for lifecycle-governance and owner-state certification.
- Daniela remains responsible for source-reliability and release certification, including her release and rollback controls.
- Riley’s periodic recheck tests evidence after packet closure but does not transfer routine closure, certification, release, or rollback authority.
- Riley’s escalation and decision role remains available for missing required fields, disputed semantics, cross-surface discrepancies, customer corrections, incident stops, and causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, or executive-language decisions.

Implementation rule

Treat January 5, 2027 as the single cutover date. Until the end of January 4, preserve the existing attendance pattern and authority boundaries. From January 5 onward, operate the delegated cadence and Riley’s bounded escalation and quarterly recheck exactly as recorded here.

arguments.title: Riley Tanaka — 2026 year-end self-review working draft
arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2026 year-end self-review working draft

First complete draft for October 16. Concise, evidence-bounded, and intended for review rather than as a polished promotion case.

1. Operating judgment and approved claim boundaries

In 2026, I made the evidence and decision boundaries explicit before allowing operating results to become leadership claims. In Q1, I kept the board-evidence lanes separate and preserved the rule that each customer-outcome row must name its denominator, cohort dates, complete predeclared outcome window, measurement limits, exclusions, source owner, reliability evidence, revenue and forecast treatment, and final claim owner. Continuous-control evidence remained labeled as continuous control coverage rather than being presented as a customer-outcome window. Missing required inputs remained not board-ready.

The approved Q1 and Q2 boundaries stayed narrow. Expansion Assist remained descriptive and noncausal, with no revenue, pipeline, or forecast treatment. Pricing-page path quality remained post-rollout continuity evidence, not a second causal test. CS auto-nudge evidence was limited to system-control and governance performance. Helio Start remained separate from the approved Q2 operating-evidence section while its mature outcome was incomplete. I did not turn preparation checkpoints, incomplete rows, or leading indicators into causal, acquisition, scale, revenue, pipeline, forecast, or board-readiness claims.

My contribution was the judgment and claim discipline: defining what each lane could support, making the denominator and window visible, and keeping exclusions attached to the claim. Owen owned reporting implementation and denominator inputs; Daniela owned instrumentation and source/release reliability; Ines owned lifecycle governance; and Customer Success operated the assisted and support paths.

2. Helio Start closeout and decision discipline

I helped keep the closed 50-workspace paid cohort in its proper category: a completed descriptive operating readout, not proof of scalable acquisition or a forecast input. The certified day-90 packet recorded 37 paid-active, 6 canceled, 4 past due, and 3 on billing hold; $56,230 in refund-adjusted collected cash; 26 minutes of median account-level support effort and 104 minutes at the 90th percentile; and 7 of 50 workspaces exceeding 90 support minutes. Paid-source attribution reconciled for all 50, and no unsupported admission entered the path.

I kept the 39-of-50 day-7 first-integration result in its proper role as a leading operating indicator, not mature acquisition or scale evidence. The fixed cohort had no randomized control, and the support tail remained material. In the August 21 decision review, I recommended neither a second Helio Start paid batch nor Q4 forecast treatment, and Priya accepted that recommendation. Paid traffic remains off; the cohort receives no pipeline or forecast credit; and no second batch opens in Q3. Before any future paid proposal, all seven high-support cases must be classified and reviewed without weakening the existing admission rules.

This was an example of changing direction through bounded judgment: I used the complete outcome packet to make a decision, but did not let complete source certification masquerade as causal evidence, commercial authorization, or forecast treatment. I also preserved the existing eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, instrumentation, and support-routing rules.

3. Leadership through delegation and retained authority

I transitioned recurring monthly preparation toward Owen’s operating lane so the team can produce the sanitized monthly campaign snapshot and board-source completeness inputs through the documented workflow and cadence. Owen’s current scope includes reporting semantics, denominators, evidence fields, preparation, routine source review, reconciliation, gap documentation, obtaining owner certifications, and recommending disposition within the established process. This is a bounded preparation and source-completeness role, not a transfer of executive-claim authority.

The October 14 authority-checklist review showed the value of that delegation without expanding the claim. Owen and Customer Success supplied a clean descriptive four-week operating read for organic onboarding: 92 admitted organic workspaces, 28 checklist exposures, and five ordinary setup-assistance requests. There was no eligibility or route mismatch, lifecycle-suppression issue, paid-source traffic, or unsupported admission, and there was no randomized control. I kept the checklist in organic onboarding and explicitly did not turn those counts into an activation claim or a support-effort claim.

I also set an explicit maintenance split for the released checklist: Ines owns lifecycle-governance and routine lifecycle-state maintenance; Daniela owns engineering implementation, release, and rollback maintenance; and I retain checklist semantics, eligibility and governed-state boundaries, exception and stop decisions, and final authority over changes that could alter claims or operating rules. The split clarifies who maintains each control without broadening anyone’s authority.

The transition is not complete delegation of my responsibilities. I still participate in routine monthly preparation and source-closure reviews; I have not left those activities. Owen may make completeness and measurement limits legible on the first pass, but missing required fields, disputed semantics, and cross-surface discrepancies remain incomplete and escalate. Until I make a separate explicit decision, preparation and recommendation do not become independent review closure, claim approval, or board-readiness authority. I retain authority over board readiness, causal or revenue claims, forecast treatment, executive language, disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, customer corrections, incident stops, state-changing work, ambiguous matters, and exception-heavy decisions. Daniela retains engineering release and rollback control, and Ines retains lifecycle-governance and her established routine review lane.

This is the leadership behavior I want to reinforce: delegate repeatable preparation and routine source review with observable boundaries, while retaining the decisions that depend on judgment, exceptions, or claims. The October 14 read demonstrated that the team could produce a clean descriptive operating packet without asking me to convert bounded counts into a stronger claim. The goal is not to eliminate my involvement by assertion; it is to earn more leverage through several reliable packets while keeping escalation explicit.

4. Organic authority-checklist release and preserved state meanings

I supported the release of the organic authority checklist as a governed operating aid, not as a new eligibility policy, blanket approval, or expansion of review authority. The release kept the existing rules legible: proceed only when every required eligibility field is current, supported, and internally consistent; hold or remain pending when required state is missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting, with the field-specific reason preserved; route for assistance before admission when the established path requires it; and refuse or route outside self-serve where the existing boundaries require it. A prior proceed decision is not portable approval after state changes or source problems.

The checklist preserved the meanings of the governed states and fields. Verified external-system authority means readiness to perform the connector’s required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action; it is not permission for automated contact or outreach. It remains distinct from connector authentication, entitlement, qualifying-human-admin status, and active Customer Success adoption or renewal work. The October 14 four-week review remained descriptive: across 92 admitted organic workspaces, there were 28 checklist exposures and five ordinary setup-assistance requests, with no eligibility or route mismatch, lifecycle-suppression issue, paid-source traffic, or unsupported admission. Those counts did not authorize changing eligibility or remedies, and they did not support activation or support-effort claims; there was no randomized control.

State-changing, ambiguous, disputed-semantics, exception-heavy, customer-correction, and incident-stop matters remain in my authority. Ines’s routine lifecycle-governance lane and lifecycle-send limits remain unchanged, and Daniela retains engineering release and rollback control. The checklist improved handoffs and operator clarity without changing the governed state meanings, eligibility or refusal rules, lifecycle-release limits, source-closure authority, or engineering controls.

Development priorities for 2027

1. Make evidence boundaries operational earlier. At the start of each evidence cycle, I will record the source, accountable owner, unit of analysis, denominator or exact coverage dates, predeclared outcome window, measurement limits, exclusions, and decision boundary in the working brief. I will require unresolved semantics, finance dependencies, or validation ownership to be visible before the first review rather than resolving them during final reconciliation.

2. Build leverage without pretending the transition is finished. I will define and review observable success criteria across the next several monthly packets: first-pass completeness, named owner certifications, reliable freshness and provenance, explicit treatment of missing or conflicting fields, and timely escalation of disputed semantics and cross-surface consequences. I will continue to participate in routine monthly preparation and source-closure reviews while testing whether Owen’s bounded preparation and routine source-review work is repeatable enough to support a future, separately decided authority change. Until then, I will not treat preparation as independent closure or claim authority.

messages.content:
30-minute 1:1 agenda: Owen — evaluating future routine source-completeness closure

Purpose

Assess whether Owen can eventually close routine, fully evidenced source-completeness reviews without Riley’s line-by-line involvement. This is an evaluation conversation only: Owen’s current preparation and reporting responsibilities remain unchanged. No new review-closure, claims, board-readiness, revenue, forecast, or executive-language authority is granted today.

0:00–0:04 — Set the boundary and objective

Say explicitly:

“Your July sanitized campaign snapshot and Q2 source lock show strong execution in your current lane. Today we are defining evidence for a possible future authority decision, not making that decision. I retain authority over board readiness, causal and revenue claims, forecast treatment, and executive language.”

Questions:
- What would “complete” mean without relying on my line-by-line review?
- Which decisions must remain outside your authority even when a packet is otherwise complete?
- How would you distinguish evidence preparation, a recommendation, and formal closure?

0:04–0:11 — Walk through the required packet standard

Use one completed packet and test whether Owen can identify, verify, and point to:

- Required denominator, or exact coverage dates where a denominator is not applicable.
- Complete, predeclared outcome window—or the exact designation “not applicable — continuous control coverage.”
- Measurement limits and exclusions.
- Source owner.
- Source or release-reliability evidence.
- Revenue treatment and explicit non-claims.
- Forecast treatment and explicit non-forecast status where applicable.
- Named owner certification for each section.
- Reconciliation across all reporting surfaces.

Questions:
- Which source directly supports each field, and what does it not support?
- Is this customer-outcome evidence or continuous-control evidence?
- What would make the row incomplete even if the headline number looks correct?
- Where is the reliability or release evidence, and how current is it?
- Who certifies each section, and what authority does that certification not convey?

Owner certification map:

- Owen: denominator or exact coverage dates, cohort/window integrity, measurement limits, and reconciliation.
- Ines: lifecycle-governance limits, suppression behavior, and exclusions.
- Daniela: source integrity, release/reliability evidence, and rollback or repair history.
- Riley: final operating-claim boundary, causal/revenue interpretation, and unresolved exclusions.
- Marcus Vail: forecast treatment.
- Tomás: final board or executive narrative, if the packet is ever proposed for that use.

0:11–0:18 — Test routine-review judgment

Questions:
- Show me how you would mark a packet incomplete rather than “mostly complete.”
- What would you do if two surfaces use different definitions or totals?
- What would you do if an owner supplies a number but does not certify the relevant field?
- How would you preserve a non-claim—for example, descriptive evidence that does not support causal, revenue, pipeline, acquisition, or forecast conclusions?
- What would you escalate rather than resolve yourself?

Expected behavior:
Owen presents the evidence, identifies the gap or disagreement, records the owner and next action, and recommends a disposition. He does not resolve disputed semantics, silently repair a source, convert descriptive evidence into a claim, or treat owner input as approval.

0:18–0:25 — Define observable evidence over the next four packets

A future authority review would require four consecutive packets demonstrating:

- 100% completion of required fields, or an explicit, justified not-applicable designation.
- 100% named-owner certification for applicable sections.
- Exact denominator or coverage dates and a valid outcome-window treatment.
- Reconciled figures and definitions across all required surfaces.
- No silent assumptions, backfills, semantic substitutions, or unsupported repairs.
-…

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Riley Tanaka, message 004945
excerpts:
1. Test first: on a scrap of the same paper, let the same cool wash dry completely. Practice with clean water until you know how much reactivation the paper tolerates.

2. Protect the edge: place a clean, dry card just beyond the structural edge and leave a narrow untouched dry buffer—about 1–2 mm. Do not wet across or undercut that boundary.

3. Rewet selectively: use a soft brush charged with clean water, then blot it until damp rather than shiny. Paint water into the pale passage, moving toward the cool shape and stopping short of the protected edge. Aim for an even satin sheen, never a puddle.

4. Soften with minimal contact: with the brush nearly dry, touch only the inner edge of the cool shape once and pull outward into the damp passage. Use one directional stroke; rinse and blot between strokes. Do not work back and forth or chase the blend.

5. Let it settle: if the transition is still too abrupt, allow it to dry fully before repeating with a narrower, lighter rewet. Don’t add pigment.

6. Dry flat and naturally: keep the crisp edge dry and shielded while the softened area dries completely. Avoid heat, airflow, tilting, and touching the surface until fully dry.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Riley Tanaka, message 001734
excerpts:
Because the eye and nose are intact, treat this as a narrow edge correction, not a general lift. The goal is to reduce the bloom’s contrast, not return the paper to untouched white.

1. Let the sheet stay completely dry and work flat.

2. Use a small, soft round or pointed synthetic brush. Load it with clean water, then blot until it feels damp rather than wet. Keep a clean, dry brush or folded tissue nearby for wicking.

3. Start at the least important section of the bloom, preferably toward the cheek rather than beside the eye or nose. Touch only the dark cauliflower ridge for a second or two. Lift vertically with the blotted brush or tissue; do not rub or drag.

4. Work in tiny sections, about 1–2 cm at a time. After each touch, allow the area to dry briefly before deciding whether it actually improved. Keep a narrow dry buffer around the eye, nose, and their surrounding shapes.

5. Once the ridge is lighter, use a second nearly dry clean brush to feather just the cheek-side perimeter. Pull outward into the existing shadow, not inward across the pale muzzle. This softens the transition without depositing the dark pigment into the light area.

6. Let it dry fully before judging it. If lifting leaves a noticeably pale notch, use one extremely dilute glaze of the existing cheek/shadow mixture over the affected zone. Keep it on the shadow side, with one soft edge and one lost edge. Do not repaint the whole muzzle.

Stopping point:

Stop after one restrained lifting pass and, at most, one feathering pass if the bloom no longer reads as a separate dark stripe at normal viewing distance. A slightly broken transition can work as fur texture in a backlit study; a perfectly uniform muzzle edge is not worth sacrificing the facial structure.

Stop immediately if:

- the paper begins to pill or feel fuzzy;
- the surrounding wash starts becoming lighter;
- pigment is spreading into the muzzle;
- the brush needs pressure;
- the eye or nose area begins to re-wet; or
- you find yourself trying to make the paper look untouched.

Avoid a wet sponge, eraser, abrasive rubbing, flooding the entire transition, or repeated rewetting. On a dry cotton sheet, preserving the surface and the intact features is more valuable than removing the last trace of the bloom.

2. Adjust the brush load: use a soft, moderately full brush, then touch it once to a cloth or paper towel. The brush should release an even film, not a visibly wet bead. Avoid repeatedly passing over the area; extra water encourages the ochre to settle into the dimples.

3. Set the board only slightly: use about a 5–10° incline, with the stroke moving consistently downward. Keep the wash moving but prevent a heavy bead collecting at the lower edge. If a bead forms, wick only the excess from the brush tip—don’t scrub the passage.

4. Apply: lay one quiet, transparent pass over the dry passage using the more diluted mix. Leave the paper untouched while it dries. If it is still too grainy, repeat with a second thin pass rather than making one stronger, wetter application.

The key combination is less pigment, controlled—not flooded—brush moisture, and a shallow incline. Yellow ochre will retain some natural granulation, but this should keep it from reading as orange or visibly lodged in the texture.

excerpts:
1. Test first: on a scrap of the same paper, let the same cool wash dry completely. Practice with clean water until you know how much reactivation the paper tolerates.

2. Protect the edge: place a clean, dry card just beyond the structural edge and leave a narrow untouched dry buffer—about 1–2 mm. Do not wet across or undercut that boundary.

3. Rewet selectively: use a soft brush charged with clean water, then blot it until damp rather than shiny. Paint water into the pale passage, moving toward the cool shape and stopping short of the protected edge. Aim for an even satin sheen, never a puddle.

4. Soften with minimal contact: with the brush nearly dry, touch only the inner edge of the cool shape once and pull outward into the damp passage. Use one directional stroke; rinse and blot between strokes. Do not work back and forth or chase the blend.

5. Let it settle: if the transition is still too abrupt, allow it to dry fully before repeating with a narrower, lighter rewet. Don’t add pigment.

6. Dry flat and naturally: keep the crisp edge dry and shielded while the softened area dries completely. Avoid heat, airflow, tilting, and touching the surface until fully dry.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Riley Tanaka, message 003818
excerpts:
Decision input: hands-on evidence-audit cadence

Scope note: This is comparison input for the proposal only. It does not approve a role change, change current owner assignments, or authorize an early operating-model change.

| Choice | Direct system contact | Duplicate work | Owner-role ambiguity | Second-approval-queue risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monthly rotating one-lane | High. Each lane receives direct inspection at least once every four months. Best for detecting silent drift, transformation defects, and stale representations. | Medium to high, especially where the audit repeats Owen’s completeness, denominator, reconciliation, or certification checks. | Medium to high. A deep recheck could look like Riley is revalidating the lane owner or reopening Owen’s closure. | High unless explicitly observational and non-gating. Teams may wait for the monthly audit before treating routine work as closed. |
| Quarterly rotating one-lane | Medium. Each lane receives direct inspection once per year if there are four lanes. Provides real system contact but leaves longer gaps between checks. | Medium to low. Less frequent overlap with routine closure work and easier to distinguish as a control observation. | Medium. Boundaries still need to say that Riley observes and documents rather than certifies, repairs, reclassifies, or approves. | Medium to low if time-boxed and non-gating. Lower risk than monthly because it is less likely to become a parallel operating process. |
| Exception-triggered only | Low and variable. It provides contact when an exception is already visible, but no baseline check for silent defects when the exception ledger is clean. | Low for routine work, but medium to high during an exception because it may duplicate the owner’s investigation and Owen’s exception ledger. | Medium to high. It can become unclear whether Riley is auditing the system, adjudicating the exception, or deciding the remediation. | Medium to high during incidents. There is no standing queue, but every sampled exception could become an ad hoc Riley decision gate. |

Assessment

1. Monthly rotating one-lane has the strongest direct-contact benefit, but it carries the greatest risk of duplicating Owen’s source-completeness work and creating a second closure process. It is only viable if the audit is explicitly a short, observational control check—not a post-closure reapproval.

2. Quarterly rotating one-lane is the safest of the three as a standing one-lane cadence. It reduces duplication and queue risk while preserving regular independent contact. Its main weakness is coverage latency: a lane could go nearly a year without direct attention, and it does not satisfy a requirement for monthly hands-on contact.

3. Exception-triggered only is efficient and useful as an overlay, but weak as the sole cadence. It is biased toward known problems and cannot detect silent drift when no exception has been recorded. It should supplement, not replace, a baseline audit.

Recommendation

If the decision must be limited to these three one-lane choices, use quarterly rotating one-lane as the standing cadence, with an existing-trigger exception override. Define it as:

“Once per quarter, Riley will conduct a small, time-boxed observation of one rotating evidence lane, tracing selected records from the source system through governed treatment and downstream representation. The observation is non-gating and does not certify the lane owner’s work, reopen routine closure, approve a claim, change a definition, or authorize a release. Existing escalation triggers remain unchanged, and a material or recurring exception may prompt an additional targeted observation.”

However, if the objective remains meaningful monthly direct system contact, the previously developed monthly cross-lane trace is better than a monthly deep recheck of one lane. It provides recurring system contact without turning Riley’s work into a duplicate completeness review or second approval queue. A narrow exception-selected trace can be included without making exception-triggered work the entire control.

Bottom line: quarterly rotating one-lane is the cleanest standing choice among the three; exception-triggered review should be an overlay; monthly one-lane should not be adopted as a routine post-closure recheck unless its non-gating boundary is enforced.

Arithmetic

- Monthly: $73 × 12 months = $876
- Twice monthly: $36.50 × 24 deposits = $876

- $73 monthly:

- $36.50 twice monthly:
  - Same annual cost, but each transfer is half as large.
  - Better matches two-paycheck-per-month cash flow.
  - After two deposits, the fund has grown by the same $73 as one monthly contribution.
  - Requires tracking 24 contributions instead of 12.

input.title: Historical Decision Card — EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger
input.body:
Decision card

Experiment: EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger
Decision point: 2023-04-03 (Riley called the experiment successful and began planning full rollout)
Decision owner: Riley Tanaka
Status at decision point: Positive / ship plan in progress; final rollout contingent on completion of final data-quality checks

Question
Should the activation-triggered onboarding touch replace the fixed calendar-day-7 touch for the in-scope mid-segment users?

Experiment design
- Scope: mid-segment users in the 50–200 seat v1 bucket.
- Treatment: key the onboarding touch off activation rather than literal calendar day 7; suppress only the existing fixed calendar-day-7 touch for treated users who had not activated. Do not suppress other lifecycle touches, activation-triggered sends, control behavior, or out-of-scope users.
- Primary metric: week-1 retention.
- Initial hypothesis: at least a +2 percentage-point improvement.
- Flag: lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2.
- Launch: March 13, after engineering review; the planned read was two weeks with target n=400.

Evidence available at the decision point
- First significant read: +2.9 percentage points in treatment, p=0.05, n=220 on that arm. Riley deliberately held rollout for one stabilization cohort rather than shipping on first significance.
- Second cohort: +3.4 percentage points in treatment, n=200.
- Pooled result across both cohorts: +3.1 percentage points treatment versus control, p=0.04, n=420.
- The direction and shape held in both PostHog and Owen’s warehouse pull, reducing concern that the first read was spurious.
- PostHog assignment was stable at first pass.

Decision
Riley called EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger positive/successful after the second cohort cleared and began drafting the ship plan with Ines. Full rollout was planned at 100% on April 10, unless the remaining checks surfaced a problem.

Why
The pooled week-1 retention lift exceeded the original +2-point hypothesis, remained positive after the stabilization cohort, and reached p=0.04 at n=420. Waiting for the second cohort was an intentional safeguard against shipping a fake first-significance result.

Open checks and conditions
Before the April 10 rollout, Owen’s pull still needed the final checks for:
- Sample-ratio mismatch (SRM)
- Signup-source mix
- Country/device skew
- Guardrail read, including activation completion and support touches

The experiment was documented as scope-disjoint from pricing_page_2023q2_rev: different cohort and metric of record. Pricing rollback-window effects were still to be ruled out as a data-quality concern, not blended into this experiment’s attribution.

Planned next steps
1. Complete the remaining SRM, mix, segment-skew, and guardrail checks.
2. Finish the ship plan with Ines.
3. If no material issue emerged, ramp lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2 to 100% on 2023-04-10.
4. After ship, watch the mid-segment post-ship cohort curve and wait for a full week before calling the post-rollout read.

Historical nuance
This card records the decision state on April 3, 2023. “Successful” meant the experiment had cleared the stabilization-cohort decision threshold and was being prepared for rollout; it did not mean every final diagnostic had already been signed off.

The $500 should be treated as neutral spending if it is ordinary spending you already planned to make. It is not an incremental cost or manufactured-spending requirement in that case.

Using the 1,800 extra points as the supplied revised marginal-reward total, the quantified comparison is:

Keep advantage = $60 credit + value of 1,800 extra points

If each point is worth p dollars:

Keep advantage = $60 + (1,800 × p)

Examples:

Point value       Value of 1,800 points       Total quantified advantage
0 cents           $0                          $60
1.0 cent          $18                         $78
1.5 cents         $27                         $87
2.0 cents         $36                         $96

Revised break-even point value

For keep-versus-downgrade break-even:

$60 + (1,800 × p) = $0

That produces:

p = −$0.0333 per point
p = −3.33 cents per point

Because points cannot have a negative redemption value, the practical break-even hurdle is therefore $0 per point, assuming:

- The $500 would have been spent anyway.
- The full $60 credit posts.
- No other differences or costs are assigned to keeping the product.

In other words, the $60 credit alone puts the keep option $60 ahead before assigning any value to the 1,800 points. If the question instead is “what point value would make the 1,800 points equal to the $60 credit by themselves,” that figure is $60 ÷ 1,800 = 3.33 cents per point. That is a comparison of the points with the credit, not the keep-versus-downgrade break-even hurdle.

One numerical caveat: the previously recorded $1,800 of travel/dining spending would generate 900 extra points from the 0.5-point-per-dollar rate difference alone. I have treated 1,800 extra points here as your revised scenario input rather than recomputing it from the earlier spending figure.

Product-retention risk

The offer is conditional on retaining the current product through the credit’s posting, not merely on completing $500 of purchases.

Relevant risks are:

- Downgrading before August 31 could forfeit the offer even if qualifying purchases have already been made.
- Completing the $500 requirement by August 31 may still not be enough; the current product must apparently remain in place until the credit actually posts.
- The credit may post in a later statement cycle because the issuer allows up to two billing cycles.
- A product change during that interval creates a direct forfeiture risk under the stated terms.
- The offer terms provided do not say whether a credit that has already posted can later be clawed back after a downgrade. That treatment would need issuer confirmation.
- The terms also do not specify whether the $500 requirement is measured by transaction date or posting date, or how returns, refunds, credits, pending transactions, and excluded transaction types affect “net purchases.”

Posting-timing risk

The main timing exposure is the gap between:

1. Making the qualifying purchases,
2. Reaching $500 in net purchases,
3. Having those purchases post and qualify,
4. Receiving the $60 credit, and
5. Being able to downgrade without forfeiting it.

A purchase made near August 31 could post after the promotional window, potentially leaving the qualifying total below $500. Even if the total qualifies, the credit could arrive one or two billing cycles later. Downgrading during that period would risk losing the entire $60, not merely delaying it.

The account-preservation terms reduce a separate risk: the downgrade is stated to preserve the account opening date, credit line, and existing points. The principal unresolved risk is therefore not loss of account history or accumulated points; it is forfeiture of the conditional credit if the product is changed before the credit is visibly posted.

Here’s a tightened, ready-to-paste version.

Opener

Helio Start is an internal exploration of how to make self-serve workable for smaller teams while protecting customers from being placed in a setup that the product, integrations, or support model cannot reliably support.

This pre-read proposes working eligibility boundaries, customer-protective non-support rules, measurement requirements, and operational dependencies for engineering scoping. It is not a final launch policy, public pricing decision, or commitment to a Q3 launch.

The baseline is descriptive, not causal: it shows current patterns in the data but does not establish why they occur. In particular, first-week integration is an observed signal, not evidence that integration alone creates activation or that Helio Start would improve activation. Any causal interpretation will require stable definitions, complete instrumentation, and an appropriate comparison design.

Risk labels

Green — Supported for current self-serve path
The product, integration, billing, and support experience appears able to serve this case reliably. Continue validation through the standard measurement and readiness checks.

Yellow — Requires validation before customer exposure
A dependency or uncertainty could make setup, product use, billing, or support unreliable. Resolve the dependency and validate the customer experience before making a customer-facing promise.

Red — Not yet supported for reliable self-serve setup
The current operating model cannot reliably support this case without a material risk of failed setup or poor customer experience. Keep it outside the self-serve path until the relevant product, engineering, lifecycle, or support capability is in place.

Language replacements

- “Bad fit” → “Not yet supported for a reliable self-serve setup”
- “Cheap plan” → “Helio Start” or “smaller-team self-serve path”
- “Refused account” → “Case we do not currently support through self-serve”
- “Ineligible customer” → “Use case outside the current supported boundary”

A short label key for the table could be:

Green: Supported
Yellow: Validate before exposure
Red: Protect customer from failed self-serve setup

results.content:
Practical checklist for June 12–15

Operating rule

- Keep this as internal self-serve operating-model discovery, not a pricing-page or Q3 launch decision.
- Treat eligibility, product constraints, lifecycle behavior, support load, and billing boundaries as linked—but do not collapse them into one “small accounts” or seat-count story.
- Mark unresolved items as gates rather than silently assuming they are launchable.

Owen — rebuild the baseline around operating complexity

By the next checkpoint:

- [ ] Split under-50 accounts by deployment shape, not only seat count.
- [ ] Add admin complexity as a separate cut:
  - [ ] One clear admin owner
  - [ ] Multiple or unclear admins
  - [ ] Permissions/workspace complexity
  - [ ] Any other operationally meaningful complexity already available in the data
- [ ] Measure whether the account completes its first integration during the first week.
- [ ] Show the interaction between first-week first integration and:
  - [ ] Activation
  - [ ] Support/contact volume, where available
  - [ ] Retention or early failure signals
- [ ] Break out the 50–75 seat band separately. Do not fold it into either the under-50 story or the 75–200 mid-segment story.
- [ ] Include activation deltas, support load, and gross retention by seat/deployment band where the data supports it.
- [ ] Document the event definitions, cohort entry point, and missing-data caveats for every cut.
- [ ] Call out which findings are descriptive baseline evidence versus conclusions about eligibility.

Deliverable:

- A compact baseline table or dashboard view with deployment shape, admin complexity, first-week first integration, and seat band as distinct dimensions.
- A short “what this changes” note identifying which account types look operationally different despite having similar seat counts.

Ines — turn the lifecycle fork map into triage

By the next checkpoint:

- [ ] Reorganize every lifecycle touchpoint into three buckets:
  - [ ] Green: safe to reuse or adapt
  - [ ] Yellow: requires an eligibility, support, or policy decision
  - [ ] Red: not safe to use yet
- [ ] Add four fields to each row:
  - [ ] Touchpoint or branch
  - [ ] Why it is in the bucket
  - [ ] Decision/dependency needed
  - [ ] Owner
- [ ] Keep reusable mechanics separate from unapproved customer promises.
- [ ] Green examples should be limited to low-risk patterns such as onboarding structure, activation-state messaging patterns, educational copy, and established email QA mechanics.
- [ ] Put support CTAs, sales-assist language, feature-specific branches, upgrade/contact-us prompts, and migration help in Yellow until the operating boundary is explicit.
- [ ] Put unsupported-feature promises, blanket “all sub-50” journeys, unchanged mid-segment eligibility logic, and production trigger/flag changes in Red.
- [ ] Confirm that the journey will not default to a state-blind calendar-day-7 branch.
- [ ] Identify the minimum decisions needed before any fork is implemented:
  - [ ] Canonical seat/eligibility definition
  - [ ] Activation-state trigger
  - [ ] Suppression and duplicate-send behavior
  - [ ] Support and Sales handoff
  - [ ] Unsupported-feature treatment

Deliverable:

- A triage view that can be reviewed row by row, rather than a general copy-edit backlog.
- No production fork, flag expansion, or trigger change until the Yellow decisions are resolved and QA is complete.

Daniela — make the scoping questions decision-ready

By the next checkpoint:

- [ ] Convert the questions into a red/yellow/green table.
- [ ] Separate each row into:
  - [ ] Eligibility decision: who may use the self-serve path
  - [ ] Product constraint: what the product can or cannot support
  - [ ] Engineering dependency: what must be built or instrumented
  - [ ] Handoff/refusal behavior: what happens when the path is unsupported
- [ ] Use refusal language that frames the boundary as protecting customers from a failed self-serve setup—not judging small accounts.
- [ ] Green: likely safe to model first:
  - [ ] Sub-50 account with an agreed seat definition
  - [ ] Single workspace
  - [ ] Standard integration path
  - [ ] One identifiable admin owner
  - [ ] No import/migration request at setup
- [ ] Yellow: needs a product or support constraint:
  - [ ] Multiple active admins
  - [ ] Import request
  - [ ] Unclear workspace ownership
  - [ ] Integration path requiring human troubleshooting
  - [ ] Billing arrangement that may require manual handling
- [ ] Red: explicit refusal or human-assisted path until proven otherwise:
  - [ ] SSO/SCIM or other enterprise controls not productized for the path
  - [ ] Complex permissions or workspace requirements
  - [ ] High-volume migration or data-cleaning work
  - [ ] No identifiable admin owner
  - [ ] Custom onboarding or bespoke implementation
  - [ ] Manual entitlement overrides
- [ ] Add the engineering questions that determine whether a row can move from Yellow to Green:
  - [ ] What event proves admin ownership?
  - [ ] Can import volume be gated before setup?
  - [ ] Which failures route to documentation versus human help?
  - [ ] What instrumentation is required before any customer-facing exposure?
  - [ ] What capacity is required, rather than absorbed sideways?

Deliverable:

- A one-pager for review that clearly labels the buckets as working inputs for engineering scoping—not final launch policy, customer-facing eligibility language, or pricing-page copy.
- Each Red or Yellow row should have an owner and a decision needed.

Billing guardrail — keep it under refusal and eligibility boundaries

- [ ] Ask the operational question: can an eligible sub-50 account start and remain self-serve using billing terms we already support, without manual exceptions or an unsafe handoff?
- [ ] If yes, document the supported billing path as part of the standard operating model.
- [ ] If no, define the refusal, Sales-assist, or human-handoff boundary.
- [ ] Do not turn the Sales Ops question into a commitment to add month-to-month billing.
- [ ] Do not redesign billing, packaging, pricing, or the pricing page as part of this work.
- [ ] Record any approved billing term as a downstream customer-facing constraint only after eligibility and operational feasibility are decided.
- [ ] Make sure Sales cannot promise custom invoicing, contract terms, or billing exceptions that Engineering, Finance, or Support have not approved.

Thread-ready guardrail:

“Billing is in scope only as an eligibility/refusal check: can a sub-50 account safely self-serve on currently supported billing terms, and where does the handoff occur if it cannot? This does not commit us to adding month-to-month billing.”

“Month-to-month offer design, billing-policy changes, pricing, and pricing-page work remain out of scope. Any approved billing term is a downstream packaging constraint, not a design premise for this discovery.”

Suggested order for the next few days

1. Owen supplies the operating-complexity baseline.
2. Daniela turns the eligibility/product questions into the red/yellow/green decision table.
3. Ines maps lifecycle branches against those decisions and marks anything blocked.
4. Resolve billing as one refusal/eligibility boundary—not as a pricing proposal.
5. Review the remaining gates: eligibility definition, supported path, refusal rules, lifecycle trigger behavior, engineering capacity, and support handoff.
6. End the week with explicit decisions, open questions, owners, and items that must not yet become customer-facing language.

input.title: January 2028 self-serve operating-model RACI
input.body:
January 2028 review

Purpose
Keep the self-serve operating model decision-ready: protect customers from unsupported setup, measure activation and support burden together, and avoid turning operating evidence into unapproved launch, pipeline, forecast, pricing, or packaging commitments.

Overall accountability
Riley Tanaka is the overall accountable owner for the self-serve operating model, including cross-surface tradeoffs, high-stakes decisions, operating-boundary changes, and executive language. Owen Pham owns routine reporting preparation and circulation; that delegation does not transfer Riley’s accountability or decision authority.

RACI

Decision area | R | A | C | I

Eligibility boundary and account segmentation | Daniela Schultz; Owen Pham | Riley Tanaka | Ines Kovac; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Product constraints and supported setup | Daniela Schultz | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Ines Kovac; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Refusal, routing, and human-assist boundaries | Customer Success; Daniela Schultz | Riley Tanaka | Ines Kovac; Owen Pham | Priya Devarajan
Billing feasibility and exception boundary | Riley Tanaka | Riley Tanaka | Customer Success; Owen Pham; Daniela Schultz | Priya Devarajan
Activation measurement and definitions | Owen Pham | Riley Tanaka | Daniela Schultz | Ines Kovac; Customer Success; Priya Devarajan
Support-load measurement and operating readout | Owen Pham | Riley Tanaka | Customer Success; Daniela Schultz | Ines Kovac; Priya Devarajan
Lifecycle states, copy, suppression, and risk controls | Ines Kovac | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Daniela Schultz; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Entitlement, support-state, and event reliability | Daniela Schultz | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Ines Kovac; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Customer-facing exposure or release readiness | Riley Tanaka | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Ines Kovac; Daniela Schultz; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Executive claims and cross-surface framing | Riley Tanaka | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Ines Kovac; Daniela Schultz; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan

Core operating outcomes

1. Activation: customers reach the defined supported-use milestone.
2. Support load: the support/contact burden created by the path, including routed or failed setup.

Weighting is 50% activation and 50% support load. They are coequal operating outcomes, not a primary metric plus a side guardrail. A strong activation result cannot offset materially unacceptable support burden, and low support volume cannot compensate for weak activation. Review both with the same cohort definitions, source-quality caveats, and segment cuts; do not combine Helio Start with retained mid-segment or Expansion Assist.

Decision rules for review

- Keep eligibility separate from product capability: an account may be eligible in principle while a workflow remains unsupported.
- Use Green / Yellow / Red working categories for scoping; they are not, by themselves, final launch policy or pricing-page copy.
- Red or unresolved Yellow cases remain outside customer-facing self-serve exposure until the relevant product, engineering, lifecycle, billing, or support dependency is resolved.
- Billing is an eligibility/refusal check against currently supported terms, not a commitment to new month-to-month billing, packaging, pricing, or custom invoicing.

document.body:
January 2028 review

Purpose
Keep the self-serve operating model decision-ready: protect customers from unsupported setup, measure activation and support burden together, and avoid turning operating evidence into unapproved launch, pipeline, forecast, pricing, or packaging commitments.

Overall accountability
Riley Tanaka is the overall accountable owner for the self-serve operating model, including cross-surface tradeoffs, high-stakes decisions, operating-boundary changes, and executive language. Owen Pham owns routine reporting preparation and circulation; that delegation does not transfer Riley’s accountability or decision authority.

RACI

Decision area | R | A | C | I

Eligibility boundary and account segmentation | Daniela Schultz; Owen Pham | Riley Tanaka | Ines Kovac; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Product constraints and supported setup | Daniela Schultz | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Ines Kovac; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Refusal, routing, and human-assist boundaries | Customer Success; Daniela Schultz | Riley Tanaka | Ines Kovac; Owen Pham | Priya Devarajan
Billing feasibility and exception boundary | Riley Tanaka | Riley Tanaka | Customer Success; Owen Pham; Daniela Schultz | Priya Devarajan
Activation measurement and definitions | Owen Pham | Riley Tanaka | Daniela Schultz | Ines Kovac; Customer Success; Priya Devarajan
Support-load measurement and operating readout | Owen Pham | Riley Tanaka | Customer Success; Daniela Schultz | Ines Kovac; Priya Devarajan
Lifecycle states, copy, suppression, and risk controls | Ines Kovac | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Daniela Schultz; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Entitlement, support-state, and event reliability | Daniela Schultz | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Ines Kovac; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Customer-facing exposure or release readiness | Riley Tanaka | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Ines Kovac; Daniela Schultz; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan
Executive claims and cross-surface framing | Riley Tanaka | Riley Tanaka | Owen Pham; Ines Kovac; Daniela Schultz; Customer Success | Priya Devarajan

Core operating outcomes

1. Activation: customers reach the defined supported-use milestone.
2. Support load: the support/contact burden created by the path, including routed or failed setup.

Weighting is 50% activation and 50% support load. They are coequal operating outcomes, not a primary metric plus a side guardrail. A strong activation result cannot offset materially unacceptable support burden, and low support volume cannot compensate for weak activation. Review both with the same cohort definitions, source-quality caveats, and segment cuts; do not combine Helio Start with retained mid-segment or Expansion Assist.

Decision rules for review

- Keep eligibility separate from product capability: an account may be eligible in principle while a workflow remains unsupported.
- Use Green / Yellow / Red working categories for scoping; they are not, by themselves, final launch policy or pricing-page copy.
- Red or unresolved Yellow cases remain outside customer-facing self-serve exposure until the relevant product, engineering, lifecycle, billing, or support dependency is resolved.
- Billing is an eligibility/refusal check against currently supported terms, not a commitment to new month-to-month billing, packaging, pricing, or custom invoicing.
- Owen may publish routine evidence independently. Riley handles exceptions, monthly operating decisions, customer-impacting boundary changes, and executive-language calls.
- Do not claim paid acquisition, pipeline, forecast, revenue, or launch expansion without a separate approval and complete evidence.

input.title: 2026 Helio Start paid-pilot high-support case review
input.body:
Date: January 1, 2028

Scope
This review covers all seven mature workspaces in the fixed 2026 Helio Start paid pilot that exceeded 90 account-level support minutes (7 of 50). It reports certified case classification and the later state/routing assessment; it does not infer causality, scalable acquisition economics, or a general product-support rate. The retained case record does not include individual workspace identifiers or per-case minute totals, so none are invented here.

Case findings
- 5 of 7: supported external-owner coordination after admission. Each required an owner-level permission or network-allowlist action for the selected connector. These are external-authority coordination cases, not ordinary integration failures.
- 2 of 7: ordinary integration troubleshooting. These were standard connector/setup issues and did not show a state-meaning or routing discrepancy.
- All 7 were reviewed; the categories are mutually exhaustive for this review.

What was ruled out across all seven
No reviewed case involved billing, an unsupported admission, stale state, or conflicting state. In all five external-authority cases, the external-authority status was current and verified yes at admission, and the governed route and lifecycle views agreed. The two ordinary-integration cases likewise showed no state-meaning or routing discrepancy.

Admission correctness
The evidence supports that the external-authority field meaning and admission decisions were correct for these seven cases. The high-support tail therefore does not, on this review, justify weakening eligibility, changing the external-authority definition, or treating valid admission as an error. The observed gap was post-admission setup sequence: a verified yes established readiness to perform the required owner action, but did not eliminate the need to coordinate that action before setup could proceed. This is a descriptive finding, not proof that a particular remedy will reduce support.

Operational follow-up
- Use a connector-specific, non-state-changing pre-setup checklist only for admitted workspaces whose selected connector requires the owner-level permission or network-allowlist action and whose status is current and verified yes.
- Keep missing, stale, conflicting, pending, no, and not-sure states on the existing fail-closed or assisted route; do not let the checklist alter eligibility, routing, lifecycle suppression, or governed state.
- Validate any checklist or setup change through replay and lifecycle preflight, and report checklist exposure separately from admission and activation outcomes.
- Continue to account for all seven cases in future paid-pilot decisions. Separate external-owner coordination from ordinary integration troubleshooting, preserve account-level support-minute reporting, and state the Customer Success staffing/capacity assumption for any capped run.

Boundary
This review supports an operational follow-up focused on setup sequence. It does not authorize another paid batch, budget, traffic, pipeline treatment, forecast credit, or an eligibility change.

Interpretation and boundary: 25 is a maximum operating bound for proposal design only. 6. Operating safeguards and stop conditions

- [ ] Eligibility and refusal rules are unchanged and documented.
